x: If you already own REAPER then the world of classical editing including source-destination editing (aka 2-, 3-, and-4-point editing), crossfade editing and more are available to you via the ReaClassical system, which is free and open source. There's no need to spend a great deal of money on Sequoia, Pyramix or SaDiE in order to make editing precise and efficient. As a classical engineer myself, I can say with certainty that what I am about to share with you covers all my recording, editing and mastering needs. Indeed, I couldn't return to the old way of working at this point. Your mileage may vary and I'd love to hear from you if there are functions that you feel might be missing.

ReaClassical 27 is the biggest release so far. The headline is complete screen reader support, but sighted engineers get a great deal too: One-click rendering from the DDP Metadata Editor to DDP, Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, Opus, MP3 and mixer stems Import DDP and PMI masters to rebuild a CD layout for checking or remastering A CD Player with Transition Review, and a Peak and Overs Check for the whole project Quick Export Recorded Takes to hand takes to musicians or the producer from the session A far more flexible Smart Import, with polywav splitting, take filtering and folder distribution options Safer editing: S-D edits automatically remove sliver edits and shorten crossfades when source material runs short A new default theme, a tidier menu and background recall of mixer snapshots This page is a short tour. Everything here is covered in detail in the relevant chapter, linked below. If you are updating from ReaClassical 26, see Update.
New Functions

Working with a screen reader ReaClassical can now be used from start to finish by a blind or low-vision engineer, with no mouse. Several parts of this are handy for sighted users too. Clara, a REAPER extension for Windows and macOS, lets ReaClassical speak through your screen reader. Install it by typing clara in the Terminal Accessible windows replace the mouse-driven ones (Create Project, Track Setup, Smart Import, Preferences, Notes, DDP Metadata Editor, Mixer Snapshots and more). Sighted collaborators can switch any of them back with Toggle GUI Mode (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G) Announcements for take number, timeline position, items in a folder, RCMASTER peak and more, with ! to repeat the last one Menu Help (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H) reads out the ReaClassical menu with the shortcut for each item Marker safety: with Clara installed, placing a source or destination IN marker after the existing OUT marker deletes that OUT marker and tells you, instead of leaving a broken pair Keyboard modes let you finish a whole task with single keys: Crossfade Mode (F) to slip, nudge, widen, narrow and shape a crossfade, Item Edit Mode (V) for one item's fades, edges and gain, and Mixer Mode (Alt+S) to mute, solo, pan, flip polarity and set faders without touching track selection. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E always returns you to the normal keys The Terminal (Ctrl+Enter): type a command such as 1m;2m;3s to mute tracks 1 and 2 and solo track 3. It also installs Clara (clara), sets nudge amounts and converts workflows. The reaper command updates REAPER itself to the version ReaClassical has been tested with (reaper=latest for the newest release, reaper=752 for a specific one). The Terminal works for everyone, with or without Clara. Type help for the full command guide See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader, Keyboard Modes and The Terminal. Every workflow chapter also has short purple Screen reader users notes. Note You do not need a screen reader to benefit from the new keyboard-driven tools below. Without Clara installed, ReaClassical behaves as it always has.

Importing Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D) rebuilds the CD track and album metadata layout from an existing DDP image, for checking or remastering Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M) does the same from a Pyramix pre-master Polywav import in Smart Import splits a multi-channel file from a portable recorder into mono and stereo tracks using a simple pattern (for example 221: two stereo pairs, then mono). It replaces the old ExplodeMultiChannel function See Importing.

Recording and monitoring Quick Export Recorded Takes (Ctrl+Shift+D) renders every take so far to WAV, FLAC, Opus or MP3, ready to hand to the producer or musicians on location Toggle Monitor (Ctrl+Shift+A) cycles input monitoring across the input tracks: off, on, tape mode Playback track: a new special track that sends the RCMASTER mix to its own pair of hardware outputs. Toggle it with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P Disarm All Tracks removes every record arm in one step Take Number Display (Alt+T) shows the current take number in a small window so a colleague can follow along See Recording.

Rendering The DDP Metadata Editor (Y) now has a row of Render buttons. Each renders straight away, without REAPER's render dialog, into an Exports subfolder: DDP (Red Book settings) and Cue Audio WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 and MP3 320, one file per CD track, with album and track metadata and cover.jpg/cover.png cover art embedded where the format allows M: Stems, one WAV per mixer track for each CD track Custom, which opens REAPER's render dialog pre-filled with your choices Sample rate, bit depth and dither are set with dropdowns, and a Tracks box (for example 1-3,5) limits which CD tracks are rendered. This online manual, located at https://reaclassical.com/manual, serves as the official documentation for ReaClassical. It is also available offline from within ReaClassical as a single HTML page by pressing H (for help). The benefit of the offline version is that it is always in sync with the version of the tools you are using. The structure of the manual is designed to take the user through preliminary remarks, install and update procedures for both ReaClassical and REAPER then a detailed look at workflows from creating a project through to final render. The Reference section follows (a keyboard shortcut guide, recommended free mastering-grade plugins, room tone generation, system tweaks for all three major OSes and frequently asked questions). I highly recommend doing a complete read of the manual and becoming very familiar with the keyboard shortcuts.
The website reaclassical.com serves as the entry point for new users. From here you can read about key features, read this manual, find installation instructions, get in touch with support and more.
It is a very good idea to have a basic fluency in how REAPER works. However, much of ReaClassical relies on different workflows than you will be used to. With that in mind:

Do Learn how items are dragged and trimmed in REAPER Continue using REAPER's mixer to set faders, panning, mute, solo (if you wish) Set up a ReaClassical project by first running Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS)

Don't Engage in any track and folder management (naming & renaming, creating, deleting, reordering etc) outside of Mission Control Set recording inputs outside of Mission Control Create custom track routing outside of Mission Control Create custom item groupings

Avoid Using regular transport controls for recording or playback Screen reader users (Clara) The same rules apply, but track and folder management is done with Accessible Track Setup instead of Mission Control. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

ReaClassical uses YY.M.MICRO versioning (where M is a non-padded month) to accurately reflect how current the software is. For example, 27.3.2 would indicate a March 2027 release with 2 further updates which might include new features, improvements to existing functions, or bugfixes. A month of 0 is used when a new year's version is released before January, since 1 would wrongly suggest January: 27.0.62, for example, is the 62nd update of ReaClassical 27 released ahead of January 2027.

ReaClassical works on top of REAPER, the digital audio workstation and utilizes ReaPack, SWS Extensions and ReaImGui. ReaClassical functions are coded using Lua. The installers for all operating systems are shell scripts (PowerShell on Windows). All coding is done either in REAPER's ReaScript Development Environment, vscode or kate on Linux. This manual is written in Markdown and built into HTML. The ReaClassical splash screen and banner are created in GIMP.

The changelog for ReaClassical functions can be found by double-clicking on the ReaClassical package in ReaPack and navigating to the History tab. For the complete and recommended experience on Linux, macOS, and Windows, run the single install script provided below. Warning You do not need to download or install REAPER separately and you shouldn't try to install ReaClassical inside an existing REAPER setup — ReaClassical comes bundled with its own fully-configured REAPER environment.

Easy Complete Portable Installation (official method) The installer script is the only official way to install ReaClassical. It sets up a self-contained REAPER together with the required extensions, the ReaClassical resource folder and the right settings in one step. Adding the ReaClassical ReaPack repository to an existing REAPER on its own is not supported. ReaPack is used only afterwards, to keep an installed ReaClassical up to date (see Updating); the installer sets that up for you. Copy the command for your operating system into either your terminal (MacOS and Linux) or PowerShell (Windows). MacOS: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://reaclassical.com/macos | sh Linux: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://reaclassical.com/linux | sh Windows: irm "https://reaclassical.com/win" | iex The installer needs an internet connection. It asks where to install (the default is your Desktop on macOS and Linux; Windows shows a folder chooser) and creates a self-contained folder named ReaClassical_<version> there. It then downloads the REAPER version ReaClassical has been tested with, the ReaClassical resource folder and the correct plugins for your operating system and processor architecture, and sets everything up. Nothing is installed system-wide. Tip Note that if the ReaClassical folder already exists, the installer will automatically add a unique suffix to ensure nothing is overwritten.

First Run Launch REAPER from the new ReaClassical folder. There is no license key, account or activation step: you can start working straight away, for example by creating your first project with Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS). Screen reader users (Clara) Install ReaClassical Clara, the accessibility bridge, by typing clara into the Terminal (Ctrl+Enter). See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Notes

Track Count A folder can contain as few as one track. Choosing a single track per folder is intended for a single stereo pair: ReaClassical still builds each folder with two tracks, but the second is kept as a hidden "spare" that can never record, so the folder structure stays consistent everywhere. Folder navigation and Mission Control skip the spare, and adding or deleting tracks later keeps it correctly hidden. Choose two or more tracks per folder for multi-microphone setups.

Workflow Choice A horizontal workflow approach means that recorded or imported takes are arranged left-to-right in a single folder. A vertical workflow approach is designed for recorded takes of similar material to be stacked vertically. Warning You cannot make folders within folders in ReaClassical. Think of it like using a digital or analogue console. There are plenty of ways to control sets of tracks including routing through submixes via Mission Control.

Mission Control As soon as you press OK, you will see the Mission Control window. Use this dialog to: Name or rename tracks Set recording inputs manually or automatically based on track naming Temporarily disable recording of a channel Set routing Add "special" tracks: aux, submix, room tone, reference, live bounce, listenback and playback (see Special Tracks below) Change visibility of folders and special tracks in the arrange window Add a track to all folders Delete a track from all folders Re-order tracks in all folders, and move aux and submix tracks up and down Convert between horizontal and vertical workflows Give mixer tracks direct connections to hardware outputs (if mixing using external gear) Warning Do not attempt to complete any of the above actions outside of Mission Control! Additionally you can use Mission Control to optionally: Reach other important ReaClassical windows via a button click Add FX, set volume, panning, mute/solo Screen reader users (Clara) Create Project and Mission Control each have a keyboard-driven equivalent: Accessible Create Project and Accessible Track Setup. Both are announced through Clara. In Mission Control the "Toggle GUI Mode" action (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G) switches between the accessible window and the standard ReaImGui window. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Special Tracks Special tracks live alongside the mixer tracks rather than inside your folders. Add them with the Mission Control Add Special Tracks button: enter how many of each you want and press OK. You can add up to 99 each of aux, submix and reference tracks, but only one each of room tone, live bounce, listenback and playback (the dialog shows "(already exists)" once you have one). The live bounce option only appears in a horizontal workflow. Once added, each special track is listed in the Mission Control Special Tracks section with mute, solo, pan and volume controls, a TCP checkbox to show it in the arrange window, a Routing button, an FX button and a delete button (RCMASTER itself cannot be deleted). Aux, submix and reference tracks can also be renamed there, and aux and submix tracks can be moved left or right in the mixer with the arrow buttons.

Aux and Submix Tracks Aux (@) and submix (#) tracks are busses that appear in the mixer only, unless you tick their TCP checkbox. Each feeds RCMASTER. ReaClassical treats them in the same way, so the difference is in how you use them: Use an aux for effects shared by many tracks, such as a reverb bus. Use a submix to collect related tracks, such as all the microphones on one orchestral section, so you can balance them together. To send a mixer track to an aux or submix, click the mixer track's Routing button in Mission Control and tick the destination. Untick RCMASTER there if the track should only reach the master bus via a submix. An aux or submix has its own Routing button too, so you can route one aux or submix into another as well as to RCMASTER.

Room Tone Track A single room tone track sits before RCMASTER, is shown in the arrange window and feeds RCMASTER. When you add it, ReaClassical imports roomtone.wav from your project's media folder onto it if one exists. Creating CD markers then trims the room tone to the length of the album and adds the fades. See Room Tone Generation and the room tone notes in the mastering section.

Reference Track A reference track (REF) sits just after RCMASTER, outside the RCMASTER structure, so it is not part of your mix. Import another recording onto it and hover over it with A to audition it and A/B against your own production. By default it is used this way; to use it as an overdub track instead, see Overdub recording and the reference track option in Preferences F5.

Live Bounce Track In a horizontal workflow, the live bounce track (LIVE) receives a send from RCMASTER and records the rough balanced stereo mix while you record the individual channels. See Live Bounce.

Listenback Track The listenback track (LISTENBACK) lets you hear a musician who is far away from the recording setup. It is shown in the mixer only, is record-armed with input monitoring on and records nothing. Choose its input channel from the dropdown in the Special Tracks section. Monitoring mutes automatically during playback and recording unless you set the monitoring JSFX to "Always On". See Listenback.

Playback Track The playback track (PLAYBACK) is a mixer-only monitoring track that receives the RCMASTER mix. It is created muted, and you choose the pair of hardware outputs it plays through from the dropdown in the Special Tracks section. Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P to unmute it when you want to monitor playback on those outputs. It does not feed the master bus.

ReaClassical has the ability to import any REAPER project (available in the top ReaClassical menu via Project Management > Convert REAPER project). Because of the dizzying amount of custom routing and folder hierachy that is possible inside a standard REAPER project, the following occurs during conversion: A new project tab is created and _converted suffix added to the RPP file Any folders are flattened Any empty tracks are deleted A single folder is formed in preparation for a horizontal workflow Any effects are moved to the relevant mixer tracks Any custom routing is removed At this point, a horizontal workflow is set up and all that is left for the engineer to do is recreate any custom routing using Mission Control. For example, if the original REAPER project used folders to organize orchestral section microphone channels, this would be recreated by clicking on the appropriate routing buttons to disconnect from RCMaster and instead route to one or more newly-created submix tracks.

Open via F5 or via Mission Control C. Use the reset button to return every option to its default. Here is a brief description for each one: S-D Crossfade Length (ms) The xfade length for all S-D edit functions. Default = 35ms. CD Track Offset (ms) The negative offset where CD markers are placed to the left of item starts. This is really for old CD players that could not process quick enough and skipped the start of audio. Default = 200ms. INDEX0 Length (s) (>= 1) If you add an exclamation mark to your CD track name in the metadata editor window, a countdown of this set length will visually appear on some CD Players. Default = 3 seconds. Album Lead-out Time (s) The amount of silence automatically set at the end of the album. Default = 7 seconds. No Auto Item Coloring To remove all automatic coloring of items, set to checked. You can still color items manually via the Colorize function K or add ranking colors via Record Panel or Notes. Default = unchecked. No Ranking Color To remove all ranking colors, set to checked. You can still color items manually via the Colorize function K. Default = unchecked. REF = Overdub Guide By default, the reference track acts as a way to A/B project material with an external reference audio file. To use as an overdub track see overdub. Default = unchecked. Add S-D Markers at Mouse Hover To avoid needing the track to be selected before placing S-D markers, set to checked. This also allows for opening the fade editor F by hover. Default = unchecked. Alt Audition Playback Rate The playrate used when using Shift+A etc. Default = x0.75. Year of Production Default = The year the project was created. CUE Audio Format The audio format that will be rendered to pair with the CUE file. Default = WAV. Floating Destination Folder For users who wish to always use the top folder as destination, this visually moves the destination folder just above the placement of source markers, making working in vertical workflow even easier without need for manual vertical scrolling. Note that when checked, the new S-D editing anywhere to anywhere is disabled and destination markers are always associated with the first folder. Default = unchecked. Find Takes Using Item Names If the audio material was not recorded in ReaClassical and the filenaming does not include a take number as a suffix, you can find takes based on item names instead by checking the option. Default = unchecked. Show Only Item Take Numbers By default, the item names show both session name (if present) and take numbers. For quicker visual location, set to checked to only show padded take numbers. Not available during the album mastering phase. Default = unchecked. Source Audition Mode By default, when setting source in and out markers, any previously existing ones are deleted. To convert previous pairs to take marker "regions" for use in the source audition manager Z, set to checked. Default = unchecked. Screen reader users (Clara) Accessible Preferences offers the same fifteen options as a keyboard-driven list: Up and Down move between options, Enter edits, Backspace resets the current option to its default and Escape closes. A "Reset All to Defaults" row restores everything. An additional "Other Settings" row holds three accessibility-oriented values: the marker/item nudge amount in milliseconds, the item edge grow/shrink amount in milliseconds (default 500) and the modifier multiplier applied by the "x modifier" versions of the nudge and grow/shrink actions.

I highly encourage the user to read the full workflows documentation for the best chance of becoming an expert in ReaClassical. However, if time is short and you have an upcoming project for which you need to learn just enough to become dangerous, read the following quick workflow summaries.

Create a ReaClassical project If not done already, create a new ReaClassical project via Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS). The number of tracks should equal the combined number of stereo and mono microphone channels. If in doubt, pick a horizontal workflow.

Quick Setup Open Mission Control via C Name your tracks. Use suffixes like "left", "R", "Pair" etc so the automatic record input button can make intelligent decisions If planning to record, manually or automatically set your record inputs Important Save your project before continuing with other workflows.

Recording Select a parent track of a folder Press F9. This opens the ReaClassical Record Panel (also available directly via Alt+Enter) and arms the selected folder. Optionally set a session name by clicking the "Session name" text beneath the take number and typing. Monitor your signal Use the left-most buttons in the panel (or F9 again) to control recording, pausing and stopping Add ranking and notes while recording or after the fact Once all recording is completed, close the record panel (automatically disengages record-armed tracks). To give the musicians or the producer the takes so far, press Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes) to export every take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320
Importing While it is always better to record in ReaClassical, occasionally you might need to use audio recorded by other engineers who used a different DAW.

Smart Import Assuming that the filenaming contains at least a track name and take number separated by underscore e.g. cello_004.wav or cello_T004.wav: Ensure that you have first created an empty horizontal or vertical workflow ReaClassical project. Copy or move source material into the media subfolder inside your ReaClassical project folder (or the custom recording path set in Project Settings P, on the Media tab). Ensure that track names in the project match the channel text in the filenames If your filenames also contain a session name prior to the track name, the items will be grouped accordingly. Via the top ReaClassical menu, click on Project Management > Smart Import Audio (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I) and, if using vertical workflow, choose distribution options. Open Mission Control to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

Manual Import by Dragging In your source folder, select items that should be aligned vertically (for example, every channel for particular take) and drag into the ReaClassical project being sure to drop onto one of the folders created by ReaClassical with a track count that matches the number of files you selected. Choose the option "Same time position on separate tracks" Continue as above for each take Open Mission Control C to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.
Auditioning Audition your material via mouse hover + A on parent or child tracks. Use mixer mute and solo buttons to further customize what you hear.

Editing Set destination IN and OUT markers via 1 and 2 Set source IN and OUT markers via 3 and 4 Press 5 to make the source-destination edit (2-, 3- or 4-point edit depending on how many markers you set), or F4 to make a time-stretched S-D edit (requires all 4 markers), or if only using destination IN marker and both source markers, F3 for an "assembly" or 3-point "insert" edit To finesse the edit, click on the right item of a crossfade pair and press F

Mixing Add FX, change routing, and optionally adjust volume, panning etc via Mission Control C For level changes over a passage (for example, pulling down a spot microphone), select the destination or source track, make a time selection and press I. Set the level and optional ramp in/out lengths and click Apply Automation. A time selection is required For "scenes" that change the whole mixer from one album piece to the next, open the Mixer Snapshot Manager via Shift+M, select an item on the first (destination) folder, adjust the mixer and click Set Snapshot.... Snapshots are tied to items and are recalled automatically during playback Before rendering, click Convert to Automation in the Snapshot Manager to turn the snapshots into real automation

Mastering The album is built on the first (destination) folder, so make sure your finished edit is there Remove all names from items on the parent track aside from those you want to be track starts. You can clear all items on the folder track via Ctrl+T Enter track start names via the Notes window N Press Y to open the metadata editor

Rendering Press Y to open the DDP Metadata Editor Choose the sample rate, bit depth and dither (and a track range if you only need some CD tracks) Click one of the Render buttons at the bottom of the window (DDP, Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, Opus 160, MP3 320 or M: Stems), or Custom to open REAPER's render dialog first. For a quick loudness and peak check, use the dry run option in REAPER's render dialog (R) Screen reader users (Clara) Every workflow above has a keyboard-driven, screen-reader-friendly equivalent. See the Accessibility section for the overview and each workflow chapter for the details.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 1. Install ReaClassical Run the install command for your operating system from a terminal (macOS and Linux) or PowerShell (Windows), exactly as described in Install. The installer prints its progress as it works, asks where to install and creates a self-contained ReaClassical_<version> folder.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 2. Install Clara Clara is the accessibility bridge that lets ReaClassical speak through your screen reader. It is available for Windows and macOS. Launch REAPER from the new ReaClassical folder. Open the Terminal with Ctrl+Enter. A single-line input box asks for a "Command:". Type clara and press Enter. Clara is downloaded and installed, any old OSARA plugin in the UserPlugins folder is removed, and REAPER restarts. From then on ReaClassical announces its actions, and its windows open as accessible, keyboard-driven versions. If you want to test announcements without Clara, the Terminal command debug=on prints them to the REAPER console and turns the accessible windows on for the current project; it is stored per project, so a new project starts with it off. Placeholder Recommended screen readers and settings for each operating system, and screen reader use on Linux, still need to be documented here.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 3. Create a project Press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS). The accessible Create Project walkthrough opens and speaks each step: An input box asks for the number of tracks per folder. The minimum is one, which creates a single stereo track per folder. Choose a Horizontal or Vertical workflow with ↑ and ↓ and press Enter. A horizontal workflow lays takes out left to right in one folder; a vertical workflow keeps like material together, with the takes of the same piece in separate, aligned folders. Neither is better (see Project Setup); you can convert later in Track Setup. For a vertical workflow, an input box asks for the number of source folders. ReaClassical then hands you straight on to Track Setup so you can name your tracks.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 4. Track Setup Track Setup is the accessible counterpart of Mission Control. Open it at any time with C. Use ↑ and ↓ to move through the menu (it wraps round), Enter to choose an item and Escape to go back. Press H for a list of the shortcuts that apply where you are. The main menu is: Track Naming: steps through every mixer track in turn so you can type a name for each. Use suffixes such as "left", "R" or "Pair" so that the automatic input assignment can work out which hardware input belongs to which track Add Track and Remove Track: add a track to every folder (leave the name empty for a default name) or delete one from every folder Reorder Track and Reorder Aux/Submix: pick up a track, move it, and put it down again; the audio and the assigned inputs move with it Special Track Naming, Add Special Track and Remove Special Track: aux, submix, reference, room tone, live bounce, listenback and playback tracks Other Commands: Convert Workflow, Connect All to RCM, Disconnect All from RCM, Auto Assign HW Outputs and Clear All HW Outputs Mixer Control: work on a mixer track's FX chain and routing Set Inputs: assign recording inputs, Auto (from the track names) or Manual Every change you make here goes through the same code as the equivalent Terminal command, so the result is identical and is confirmed aloud. As in Mission Control, do all track management here and never directly in REAPER. See Mission Control for what each of these does.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 5. Set your preferences Press F5 to open Accessible Preferences. ↑ and ↓ move between options, Enter edits one, Backspace resets it to its default and Escape closes. A Reset All to Defaults row restores everything, and an Other Settings row holds the nudge amount, the item edge grow/shrink amount and the modifier multiplier. See Preferences.

t: Getting Started with a Screen Reader
x: 6. Finding your way around H inside a window lists that window's shortcuts for you to step through one at a time. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) walks through the whole ReaClassical menu, announcing the shortcut beside each item. Up and Down browse a level, Enter opens a submenu or runs an item and Escape steps back. ! repeats the last announcement. Terminal help opens the full Terminal command guide. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E (Exit Mode) always returns you to the normal keys from any keyboard mode. Alt+K (Panic Mute) silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs, and unmutes only what it muted. If a window loses focus, pressing its shortcut again closes it and opens a fresh, focused one.

Everything the Record Panel does for sighted engineers is done for you by the Record Panel Daemon, a background process that keeps the take counter, the session name and the schedule, and speaks the result of each action. You never need to open or use the Record Panel itself.

Before You Record Make sure every track has a recording input. Open Track Setup (C) and choose Set Inputs: Auto assigns inputs from the track names (suffixes such as "left", "R" or "Pair"), Manual lets you choose each one. If you try to record without any inputs set, you hear "No inputs set -- please assign inputs before recording". Optionally set the session details in Accessible Recording Settings (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R). It lists the session name, the take number, the scheduled start, end and duration, and switches for allowing takes anywhere, recording takes horizontally and clip reporting, plus a row to start or stop the daemon. Move with ↑ and ↓ and press Enter to change a row. Changing the session name resets the take number to 1, and switching to an existing session name works out the next take number from the takes already recorded. Select the parent track of the folder you want to record into.

Recording Everything is driven by F9: The first press starts the daemon (if it is not running) and arms the folder. You hear "Armed for take 12", or "Folder armed" if there is no session take counter to report. The second press starts recording: "Recording take 12". The next press stops it: "Recording Stopped". There is no need to position the edit cursor first: arming moves the recording position to after the final item in the armed folder. During a recording: Shift+F9 increases the take number, useful after a false start Alt+F9 starts the next recording section. In a vertical workflow this arms the first source folder, and in both workflows it places the edit cursor 5 seconds after the final item in the project. With "record takes horizontally" on, it arms the next folder down instead Ctrl+F9 pauses Alt+A announces the take number, Shift+T the highest take, and Ctrl+Shift+J the timeline position M adds a marker A restricted set of keys is active while you record, so that nothing disruptive can be pressed by accident. See Recording mode.

h: Sending Every Take to Someone on Location
x: Sending Every Take to Someone on Location Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes) exports every take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320, to share with musicians or a producer. It has two rows, Render Settings and Export. See Distributing Takes On Location.

Ranking and Notes After a take, select its item on the parent track and open Item Rank with Ctrl+R. The list is circular: No Rank, Excellent, Very Good, Good, OK, Below Average, Poor, Unusable and False Start. ↑ and ↓ move through it, Enter applies the highlighted rank and Backspace clears it. The window stays open, so you can rank several items in one sitting: ← and → (or Q and W) move to the previous and next item, Space plays and stops, and Escape closes it. The Terminal command ir= sets a rank too. Item notes, project and track notes, the item name and the take number are in the accessible Notes window (N), and Shift+N opens a quick Item Name window. See Typing Notes.

Special Tracks While Recording Add a live bounce track (horizontal workflow only) to record a rough stereo mix alongside the individual channels, or a listenback track to hear a musician far from the recording setup, from Track Setup under Add Special Track. Listenback monitoring mutes automatically during playback and recording.

Monitoring and Playback Ctrl+Shift+A (Toggle Monitor) cycles input monitoring on all input tracks that are not disabled for recording, and announces the new state: "Monitor: off", "Monitor: on" or "Monitor: tape mode" Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P (Toggle Playback) mutes or unmutes the playback track ("Playback unmuted" or "Playback muted"). The track is created muted. If there is no playback track you are told so M adds a marker while recording, which you can later use to split a take into subtakes with Shift+S; Alt+M gives a marker a name Alt+T (Take Number Display) opens a small window showing the current take number for a sighted colleague. The daemon opens it automatically

Finishing When all recording is done, press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9 (Close Recording Session) to stop the daemon. This disarms the record-armed tracks, the same as closing the Record Panel does for sighted users. The Disarm All Tracks action does the same job for the tracks alone, and you can always switch the daemon off from Accessible Recording Settings.

h: Checking Your Levels and Disk Space
x: Checking Your Levels and Disk Space Alt+P announces the RCMASTER peak level. In Mixer Mode, Enter announces the current mixer track's status and I its input The Accessible Audio Calculator works out the disk space needed for a duration of audio, or the time available on a given amount of disk, from units, channel count, sample rate, bit depth and format Track peaks are announced as you move between tracks with ↑ and ↓
Smart Import brings in audio files that are named with a track name and a take number. The screen reader route is a spoken wizard with the same options as the sighted window.

Preparing the Files Follow the file naming rules in Importing: the take number comes last, preceded by an underscore (cello_012.wav or morning_cello_T012.wav), and the part before it is split at underscores into an optional session name and the track name. Put the files in the project's media folder, or the recording path set in REAPER's Project Settings (P), and make sure you have already created a ReaClassical project.

Running Smart Import Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I. ReaClassical announces "Scanning files in project media folder" and then "Scan complete". If the folder also contains multi-channel files, you are first asked to choose between Import Takes and Import Polywav, using ↑ and ↓ and Enter; otherwise it goes straight to the takes wizard. The takes wizard offers, in turn: Track name order: if the project's tracks have no names yet, this assigns the names found in the filenames to the tracks. The list is in the order the names will be assigned. Pick an entry up, move it up or down and drop it, as in Track Setup's Reorder Track; entries moved past the divider are "not used this run" Distribution (vertical workflow only): One folder per take, Use current folder count, or Round-robin across a custom number of folders (you are asked for the number, with a minimum of 1), and the starting folder Import only these takes (optional): a session name, and a list of takes such as 1-3,5,11-15 A final confirmation step before anything changes in the project Material is inserted at the edit cursor, and files that are already used in the project are ignored. Afterwards, open Track Setup to add aux and submix tracks and adjust the routing.

h: Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder
x: Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder Choose Import Polywav to split multi-channel files into mono and stereo tracks. Name the files [sessionname_]Txxx.wav, and enter a channel composition pattern of the digits 1 (mono) and 2 (stereo), for example 221. Enter opens a box to set the pattern (keep or change it there), and ReaClassical tells you how many tracks it gives or why it can't be used. A usable pattern moves on, with the same distribution options as the takes wizard in a vertical project, and a final Enter imports. If the media folder contains only multi-channel files, you go straight to this step. See Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder for how the pattern is applied.

Other Imports Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D) and Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M) rebuild an album layout from an existing master in a fresh project with an empty destination folder The Terminal command import= runs a Smart Import without the wizard. See The Terminal

x: Project Tabs Ctrl+Alt+N opens a new project tab and Ctrl+Tab moves to the next one, announcing its name. Use separate projects or tabs for the discs of a multi-disc album.
Auditioning means hearing a folder, or the area around your editing markers, without touching the mouse.

Hearing a Folder Choose the folder with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D (see Navigating a Project). Moving to a folder makes it the audible one, so there is nothing else to switch. Then: Space plays and stops Shift+Space plays and stops, moving the edit cursor along with the playhead Ctrl+Shift+Space returns to the position where you last stopped In Mixer Mode, S solos the current mixer track and Shift+S unsolos everything.

h: Hearing the Area Around Your Markers
x: Hearing the Area Around Your Markers Once you have set source and destination markers, each of these selects the right folder, makes it audible and plays a short segment, announcing a message if a marker is missing: Shortcut Plays 6 / 8 3 seconds from the destination IN / OUT marker 7 / 9 3 seconds from the source IN / OUT marker Ctrl+6 / Ctrl+8 the 3 seconds up to the destination IN / OUT marker Ctrl+7 / Ctrl+9 the 3 seconds up to the source IN / OUT marker Alt+6 or Alt+8 from the destination IN to the destination OUT marker Alt+7 or Alt+9 from the source IN to the source OUT marker Starting a new audition stops any audition still playing. Use Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. to nudge a marker after hearing it, then audition again.

Auditioning a Crossfade In crossfade mode (F with Clara installed), Z plays 1.5 seconds either side of the crossfade, X plays the left item up to the center and C plays from the center of the right item. Hold Ctrl or Shift with the key for a longer, 3 second version. See Keyboard Modes. Note The mouse-hover audition keys, A and Shift+A (which plays at the custom audition rate), find the folder and position from the mouse pointer, so they are not available from the keyboard. A keyboard version is planned.

Source-destination (S-D) editing is fully keyboard-driven, and every marker and edit action is announced. This chapter follows the editing workflow; the full descriptions of each function are in Editing.

h: Placing Markers and Making an Edit
x: Placing Markers and Making an Edit Select the folder where you want to place the marker pair (moving to it with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D selects it), then: Place the destination IN and OUT markers with 1 and 2 Place the source IN and OUT markers with 3 and 4 Press 5 for the source-destination edit, F4 for a time-stretched edit (all four markers) or F3 for a 3-point insert edit Hear the result with the audition keys in Auditioning with a Screen Reader: 6 to 9 play around each marker and Alt+6 / Alt+7 play between a pair Each marker announces its position, for example "Added source in @ 1 minute 23 seconds". If you place a marker on the wrong side of its partner (a source OUT before the existing source IN, say), the stale partner is deleted and you are told so, which stops an edit silently taking far more material than you intended. To move the edit cursor to a marker use Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4. Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. nudge a marker left or right by the nudge amount after you have auditioned it; set the amount with the Terminal command nudge=10 (in milliseconds). Ctrl+Delete deletes all S-D markers. You can also set both source markers to the edges of the selected items with F12, or the destination markers with Ctrl+F12.
Deleting Backspace deletes the material between the source IN and OUT markers and ripples later material back with a short crossfade. Ctrl+Backspace deletes it and leaves the silence in place.

Fixing Up the Crossfade With the right-hand item of the crossfade selected, press F to enter crossfade mode, the keyboard version of REAPER's two-lane editor. It gives you slip, nudge, shift, widen and narrow, fade length and shape, volume, audition and reset and revert, all announced. See Crossfade Mode for the keys. Alt+Q and Alt+W jump between crossfade groups. If items that should be grouped have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder (for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items), select any one of them and press Shift+X (Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits). Use ↑ and ↓ to pick which track has the correct edits, Enter to run the fix and Escape to cancel.

Working on a Single Item Item Edit Mode (V) edits one item's fades, edges and volume from the keyboard. See Item Edit Mode. Shift+R opens the accessible Playback Rate window, which changes an item's rate (rippling the following items) or its pitch. Press H in it for examples.

Nudging Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. nudge the selected marker left and right (each audition from or to a marker selects it automatically), and Alt+, and Alt+. nudge the selected items. Each nudge is announced, for example "Mozart take 3 nudged 10 milliseconds left". The larger "x modifier" versions are Ctrl+Alt+, and Ctrl+Alt+. for markers and Alt+< and Alt+> for items. Set the nudge amount with the Terminal command nudge=10 (milliseconds) and the multiplier with mod=10, or under Other Settings in Accessible Preferences. In crossfade mode, the crossfade nudge keys are used instead and you are reminded of that.

Other Editing Functions Ctrl+H heals a patch edit, restoring the underlying material without splits ("Edit healed") Ctrl+F finds the source material of an edited item and places a source IN and OUT marker pair there, announcing "Source found" with the take X crossfades two overlapping items when the edit cursor is in the overlap Shift+F removes the fades from items whose edges are not part of a crossfade ("Non-overlapping item fades removed"), Ctrl+V pastes and announces how many items were pasted, and Ctrl+Alt+A selects all items in the folder Ctrl+Alt+C and Ctrl+Alt+M copy or move the destination material into a new source folder, and Ctrl+Alt+P promotes a source folder to the destination Shift+K re-applies the automatic item colors; with a screen reader, colors matter less, but take numbers are still extracted for Enter (find take) Multi-project-tab editing uses Ctrl+Alt+1 to Ctrl+Alt+4 to set project markers in other tabs; see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing Note The Source Audition Manager (Z) is a mouse-driven window and is blocked while the accessible windows are active. A keyboard version has not been written; use the S-D marker keys and the audition keys to compare alternative source takes.
This chapter follows the mixing workflow. The mixer itself is controlled with Mixer Mode, the snapshot manager and the automation windows are keyboard-driven, and every change is announced.

Setting Up the Mixer Use Track Setup (C) to add FX chains, routing, aux and submix tracks and hardware outputs. Open a track's FX chain or routing from Track Setup's Mixer Control, or from Mixer Mode with F and R. See Getting Started with a Screen Reader.

Mixer Mode Press Alt+S for Mixer Mode. ↓ and ↑ move between the mixer, aux, submix and other special tracks, and a single key changes the level, pan, mute, solo or polarity of the current track without touching REAPER's track selection. Grouping keys build groups of tracks. See Mixer Mode for every key. Press Enter to hear the current track's status and I its input.

Mixer Track Grouping The accessible Mixer Track Grouping window manages groups of mixer tracks. ↑ and ↓ browse the groups and a New group row creates one. Enter opens a group, where you can rename it, choose which special tracks are members and switch on or off whether each of mute, solo, pan, fader, automation and polarity fans out across the group.

Mixer Snapshots Snapshots are mixer scenes tied to items on the first (destination) folder. To capture one quickly, select an item on the first folder and press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S (Snapshot Add) Shift+M opens the accessible Snapshot Settings, which covers the same ground as the sighted Mixer Snapshot Manager: the bank picker, adding and updating a snapshot, browsing, recalling, deleting and annotating existing snapshots, the recall settings (auto-recall, the gap folder, the nine per-parameter recall switches, switching mid-gap and background auto-recall) and converting to or clearing automation Before you render, convert to real automation. Snapshots recall in real time and are unreliable in a faster-than-realtime render See Mixing for how recall, banks and conversion work.

Volume and FX Automation I opens the Automation Navigator, a keyboard walkthrough for inserting automation over a time selection. Make a time selection first. You choose the track (press Shift+Enter to toggle several tracks and apply to them in one pass), then the envelope or FX parameter, then the level and optional ramp in and out. You hear the level you are choosing while you dial it in, but ramps cannot be previewed. Ctrl+I opens Edit Automation for an existing automation item. Alt+D and Alt+E show and hide automation lanes, Shift+← and Shift+→ move between automation items and Ctrl+Shift+↑ and Ctrl+Shift+↓ move between envelope lanes. The first time you create an automation item, ReaClassical turns on automation mode, which locks the source-folder items and sets ripple editing to all tracks, so a ripple edit on the destination carries the automation along.

Hardware Outputs and Panic Mute Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T toggles the mute on RCMASTER's own hardware output sends. If any is unmuted it mutes them all, and it only unmutes when all are muted. Alt+K is Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs and later unmutes only the tracks it muted itself. It is available in every keyboard mode.

Checking Levels Alt+P announces the RCMASTER peak level Shift+P opens the accessible Peak and Overs Check, which announces the peak position and the number of overs, moves the edit cursor to the peak and lets you browse the overs The Terminal has fast level commands, such as setting a fader or muting by track number. See The Terminal

ReaClassical has several keyboard modes for screen reader users. Each mode swaps in its own set of single-key shortcuts for one kind of task, so a whole task can be done from the keyboard with every action announced through Clara. Only one mode is active at a time, and the keys listed below work only inside that mode. Crossfade Mode, started with F: edit a crossfade Item Edit Mode, toggled with V: edit one item's fades, edges and gain Mixer Mode, toggled with Alt+S: mix without touching track selection Recording mode, entered automatically while recording: a restricted, safe set of keys In every mode, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E (Exit Mode) returns you to the normal keys, and it is safe to press if you are not sure which mode you are in. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) opens a browsable list of the ReaClassical menu with the shortcut for each item, and Alt+K toggles Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs (it only unmutes what it muted itself). Space plays and stops, and Q and W move between items, in the same way as outside the modes. Note Item Edit Mode and Mixer Mode need Clara. Sighted users work with item fades and the mixer directly, and use REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor in place of Crossfade Mode.

Crossfade Mode Press F with the right-hand item of a crossfade selected. ReaClassical treats the selected item as the crossfade's right-hand item, and the left-hand item is the one whose end crossfades with it. It selects both of them and their peers across the folder and turns on ripple-per-track until you leave the mode. If the selected item is not the right-hand item of a crossfade, you are told so. Press F again to leave. This gives the same control as REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor, which is used instead when Clara is not installed. Most keys act on the selected side of the crossfade: select the left item (S), the right item (D) or both (A). Keys Action A / S / D Select both / the left / the right item Z / X / C Audition the crossfade (1.5 s either side of its center) / the left item up to the center / the right item from the center Ctrl+Z or Shift+Z, Ctrl+X and so on The same auditions with twice the length (3 s) ← / → Slip the item's audio left / right (downstream material ripples) Ctrl+← / Ctrl+→ Nudge the item left / right J / K Shift the crossfade left / right (no ripple) I / U Widen / narrow the crossfade P / O Grow / shrink the start of the fade ] / [ Grow / shrink the end of the fade T Cycle the fade shape N / M Match the right item's fade-in to the left item's fade-out / the reverse ↑ / ↓ Raise / lower the selected item's volume by 1 dB (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓ for 0.2 dB, Ctrl+0 to reset) 0 Reset both fades to a 35 ms equal-power crossfade Ctrl+Alt+0 Revert the crossfade to how it was when you first edited it this session Slips, nudges, shifts, widening, narrowing and fade changes all move by the project nudge amount (set it with the Terminal command nudge=20, in milliseconds). Most actions also have a larger "x modifier" version on the same key with Shift or Ctrl added (for example Shift+← or Ctrl+J), which moves by the nudge amount multiplied by the modifier amount (Terminal command mod=10). Some actions are blocked when both items are selected, because they only make sense for one side. Each keyboard crossfade action announces what it did, and the Announce Selected Items action tells you whether the left item, the right item or both are selected. Outside crossfade mode, Alt+Q and Alt+W jump between crossfade groups.

Item Edit Mode Toggle with V. The mode works on the item that is currently selected, and follows the selection: move to another item with any navigation key (Left, Right, Q, W or a click) and the mode announces the new item and which side of the fade is active. Press V again to leave. Keys Action S / D Choose the fade in / the fade out as the active side I / U Grow / shrink that fade T Cycle the fade shape 0 Reset the fade P / O Grow / shrink the left edge of the item ] / [ Grow / shrink the right edge of the item ↑ / ↓ Raise / lower the item's volume by 1 dB (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓ for 0.2 dB, Ctrl+0 to reset) Ctrl+S Save the project Holding Shift with a growing or shrinking key (for example Shift+I or Shift+P) uses the larger "x modifier" amount. Edges move by the Item Edge Grow/Shrink Amount (default 500 ms), and the modifier multiplier applies on top. Set both in Accessible Preferences under Other Settings.

Mixer Mode Toggle with Alt+S. Mixer Mode acts on a current target, a mixer, aux, submix or other special track that you move between with ↓ and ↑. It never changes REAPER's real track selection, so folder, item and take navigation carries on as normal while you mix. Press Alt+S again to leave. Ctrl+G removes the current group and Ctrl+Shift+G removes all groups. Navigation also works inside Mixer Mode: Alt+↓ and Alt+↑ move between folders, Shift+D goes to the first folder, and Q and W move between items.

Recording Mode While a recording is in progress, ReaClassical automatically switches to a restricted set of keys, so nothing disruptive can be pressed by accident. The keys available are: Keys Action F9 Stop recording Shift+F9 Increment the take number Ctrl+F9 Pause Alt+A / Shift+T Announce the take number / the highest take Ctrl+Shift+J Announce the timeline position M Add a marker S Split items at the cursor E Show or hide children Ctrl+Alt+→ and similar Zoom to the whole project Alt+S Mixer Mode (leaving it returns you to Recording mode) Ctrl+Enter The Terminal Zoom and view keys are available too. Stopping the recording returns you to the normal keys.

The Terminal is a single text-entry dialog opened with Ctrl+Enter. Type a command, press Enter, and ReaClassical carries it out and speaks a confirmation. It is built for screen reader use and covers fast power-mixer moves (mute, solo, pan, fader, peak, polarity), workflow conversion, importing audio, nudge and modifier amounts, and setup utilities. You can run several commands at once by separating them with a semicolon: 1m;2m;3s mutes tracks 1 and 2 and solos track 3.

Setup Commands Command What it does clara Download and install Clara (Windows and macOS), then restart REAPER reaper Install the REAPER version ReaClassical has been tested with. reaper=latest installs the newest public version and reaper=752 (for example) a specific one debug=on / debug=off Also print announcements to the REAPER console. Stored per project help Open the full Terminal command guide in your browser

Full Command Guide The complete list of commands, with the target syntax used to select tracks, aux and submix tracks, the RCMASTER and reference tracks, is in the Terminal Command Guide. It is also installed with ReaClassical and opens when you type help.
Now that you have decided on a workflow, we can start recording!

Manually Setting Inputs Use Mission Control C to set recording inputs and panning manually or automatically based on track name. For automatic assignment, add text like "Left", "R", "Pair", "2ch" etc. as a suffix and press Auto Rec Inputs.

Primary and Secondary Recording Paths By default, ReaClassical creates a media subfolder within the project directory to serve as the primary location for storing audio files. If a secondary recording folder is specified, all tracks are automatically configured to use it. To set the secondary recording path or change the primary path, open Project Settings by pressing P, then select the "Media" tab.

Easy Steps to Record Select a parent track of a folder Press F9. This opens the ReaClassical Record Panel (also available directly via Alt+Enter) and arms the selected folder. Optionally set a session name by clicking the "Session name" text beneath the take number and typing. Monitor your signal Use the left-most buttons in the panel (or F9 again) to control recording, pausing and stopping Add ranking and notes while recording or after the fact Once all recording is completed, close the record panel (automatically disengages record-armed tracks). Screen reader users (Clara) No panel is needed: pressing F9 starts the Record Panel Daemon, which runs in the background and keeps track of everything the Record Panel does for sighted users (take counter, session name, scheduled recording and so on). Press F9 to arm the selected folder, again to start recording and again to stop. Hear the current input and status with the Mixer Mode announcement scripts, and use ! to repeat the last announcement. Set the session name, take number, scheduled start/end/duration, overlapping takes, horizontal takes and clip reporting in Accessible Recording Settings (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R). When recording is finished, close the daemon with Close Recording Session (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9). See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader for setting up Clara. Tip There's no real need to position the edit cursor before starting to record as the arm/record function will automatically move the recording start position to after the final item in the armed folder.

Distributing Takes On Location When you are recording on location, you can hand every take recorded so far to the musicians or the producer without leaving the session. Use Distribute Takes (Ctrl+Shift+D, called Quick Export Recorded Takes in the ReaClassical menu). It builds one region per take (for each folder, in either workflow) and renders each one through the mixer to the master as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320, using the sample rate, bit depth and dither you choose for WAV and FLAC (Opus and MP3 keep their own fixed settings). The files go into a subfolder of Exports/Distribute_Takes named for the format and settings, so exporting again at a different rate or format never overwrites an earlier export. Folders other than the one being rendered are muted for each pass, and your mute states are restored afterwards. Screen reader users (Clara) Ctrl+Shift+D opens an accessible version with two rows, Render Settings (sample rate, bit depth, dither) and Export (choose the format and press Enter to render at once). It always exports every take; there is no track-range prompt.
Additional Notes on Record Panel

Session Names and Take Numbers To set a session name, click the greyed "Session name" text beneath the take number in the Record Panel (only possible while stopped), type a name and press Enter (or click elsewhere). Press Esc to cancel. To remove the name, click it, delete the text with backspace and press Enter. Note that if you create a new session name, the take number will automatically be reset to 1. If you switch to an existing session name with recorded takes, the take number will be calculated accordingly.

Ranking and Notes During recording, any ranking or notes added will affect the item created immediately after recording finishes. When transport is stopped, if no items are selected, ranking and notes affect the last recorded items. Apply ranking and notes to previous items in the timeline by selecting them.

h: Other Buttons and Options in the Main Window
x: Other Buttons and Options in the Main Window Click the take number (after confirming) to recalculate the take count, and use the Settings button for the options described in Record Panel Settings. Use +Take (Shift+F9, also while recording) to quickly increase the take number (useful for a false start, for example). Press Next (Alt+F9) to start a new recording section. This means that in vertical workflow the first source folder is rec-armed and in both workflows, the edit cursor is placed 5 seconds after the final item in the project. Enable "Record Takes Horizontally" while in vertical workflow to record takes left to right on a single folder. This is useful, for example, if you prefer to have each folder contain takes for just one piece of music. In this instance, Next acts as a sort of carriage return and arms the next folder down as well as move the edit cursor to the start of the timeline (or after any existing material).
Record Panel Settings Click the Settings button in the Record Panel to open a popup with the take number, scheduled recording and take placement options described below.

Allow Take Recording Anywhere This setting overrides the default safety feature of only allowing new recorded items after the final item on the folder. This is useful if you record musical material out of order and wish to place new items at an arbitrary position on the project timeline.

Scheduled Recording To start (and optionally end) a recording at specific times or manually start a recording to end at a certain time or after a certain duration, click the Settings button on the Record Panel window and add the appropriate entry or entries in HH:MM format. After pressing Apply, the Record Panel window will display information above the take number. If you enter a start or end time earlier or equal to the current time, the function will assume a next day schedule and will annotate the time with an asterisk (*). Likewise, with both a start and end time, if the end time is earlier than or equal to start, it will assume a time 24 hours later. Don't forget to arm your tracks before walking away!

Overriding Take Numbers You shouldn't need to use this but there are cases where you might want to start a new ReaClassical project but continue from the previous day's last take number. To do so, check the "Allow Take Number Override" option and set a new take number. Note that it will not allow you to set a number lower than already used.

Remote Recording via web interface The ReaClassical Remote is a browser-based control panel that mirrors the Record Panel's core functionality, allowing you to arm tracks, start and stop recording, manage takes, and apply rankings and notes from a phone, tablet, or laptop anywhere in the room. To set it up, enable REAPER's built-in web remote by opening REAPER preferences O and navigate to Control/OSC/web and add a new web browser interface from the drop-down. Select ReaClassical_remote.html from the default interface drop-down and click apply. This same options page displays a ready-made access URL. Simply open that in a browser on any device connected to the same local network. Once connected, the Arm/Rec/Stop button, Pause/Disarm, +Take, and Next Section buttons all behave identically to their counterparts in the Record Panel window, and the take number display is kept in sync with the running panel. Session settings including start and end times, duration, and session name are read from REAPER on first load and can be edited and applied back to the running panel from the Session Settings section at the bottom of the page. Rank and notes can be set remotely and will be applied to the last recorded items exactly as if you had used the Record Panel directly. Note that the Record Panel Lua script must be open and running for the remote to function correctly, as it acts as the bridge between the web interface and ReaClassical's project state.

Meterbridge Use B to open the Meterbridge. The default view shows numeric peak holds. When tracks are record-armed, the main window displays recording inputs. During auditioning of material, the top rows show mixer tracks and the bottom any special tracks including RCMASTER and Master tracks. To switch to graphical meters, check the "Graphical Meters" option. Under the options tab, you can set color thresholds for yellow and red. To switch to channel numbers instead of hardware names, uncheck the option while tracks are rec-armed.

Recording Indicator The recording indicator (Alt+R) is designed to be placed on a secondary monitor full screen so in situations where engineers are located in a separate control room, musicians are aware of when recording is active. Right-click to set custom colors for offline, standby, recording and pause.

Live Bounce To record the rough balanced mix as a stereo file at the same time as individual channels, add a live bounce track via Mission Control. Note that this is only available in a horizontal workflow given the necessity to record left-to-right on the time line to align with the folder recording.

Listenback To hear verbal feedback from a musician far away from the recording setup (for example, an organist in a loft), add a listenback track via Mission Control. Set the desired input channel via the dropdown. Monitoring will automatically mute during playback and recording. To set monitoring to always on, open the FX panel on the listenback track and set the dropdown in the monitoring JSFX to "Always On".

Splitting items into subtakes To split a selected item into numbered subtakes, add generic markers via M at the desired locations and press Shift+S to split. To name a marker, press Alt+M (REAPER's insert and/or edit marker) and use the name instead of subtake numbering. Ctrl+M deletes the marker nearest the edit cursor, Ctrl+Shift+M moves the nearest marker to the edit cursor and Ctrl+Shift+G deletes all generic markers.

Monitoring and Playback Toggle Monitor (Ctrl+Shift+A) cycles input monitoring on all the input tracks that are not disabled for recording: off, on, then tape mode. The new state is announced. Toggle Playback (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P) mutes or unmutes the playback track (see Navigating a Project). The playback track is created muted, so this unmutes it for monitoring. Take Number Display (Alt+T) shows the current take number in a small window. It is started automatically by the Record Panel Daemon in the screen reader recording workflow, so that a sighted colleague can see the current take.

Headroom REAPER's peak indicators are reset automatically each time recording starts, so the peak values you see afterwards belong to the current take. Again, I refer you to the books on classical music production but in general I suggest aiming for around -12dB peaks on the meters. 24-bit recording allows for a lot of headroom so there's no need to push close to 0dB. Adjust the individual mixer track faders to balance. When using a 32-bit float device with dual AD converters as an interface (such as the Zoom F-series), ensure that the recording file format is switched to 32-bit float via project preferences P. The recorded levels might seem too low or too high during recording, but they can be easily adjusted afterward in ReaClassical without introducing any extra noise or distortion.

Recording Safety When using the Record Panel for recording (essential!), there is increased safety when using classical take recording via the automatic switch to a restricted set of keyboard shortcuts. In addition to using the record panel, you can also access various non-disruptive functions like zooming.

Overdub Recording To record additional material after the fact (say a separate narration track or an organ part in a church after the main recording session in a concert hall), edit the orchestral material as usual and use a mixdown as a guide track in a new project (or new project tab). To achieve this, use a vertical workflow (convert if necessary via Mission Control C), add a Reference track also via Mission Control and set the ReaClassical Project Preferences option REF = Overdub Guide to checked (F5). With this setting, audio on the guide track will be audible during take recording and auditioning of folders. Use Classical Take Recording via the Record Panel as normal. You can then S-D edit and mix the overdub material to fit with the orchestral mixdown or, if further mixing and mastering work is required on the original multi-track material, bring the organ part into that project as a new track in the folders (see below).

h: Manipulating Tracks During a Recording Session
x: Manipulating Tracks During a Recording Session Screen reader users (Clara) Use Accessible Track Setup to add, delete and reorder tracks (including aux and submix tracks) from the keyboard instead of Mission Control.

Disabling Channels In a typical recording session, the musicians with the least to record are often allowed to leave the session early once their work is completed. If they were individually recorded using a spot microphone, it wouldn't make sense to continue recording on that channel. The ReaClassical way, both easy and visually obvious, is to open Mission Control C and check "Rec Disabled" for the particular channel(s). When arming and recording, these channels will now be excluded. This allows the user to maintain hardware connections that were originally set up with the ability to quickly bring the microphone back in as required.

h: Adding a New Microphone Mid-Recording Session
x: Adding a New Microphone Mid-Recording Session You can add a track to all folders in the project at once via Mission Control. It will prompt you for a name and then add a new track with that name to the end of each folder. This also works for a single folder while working in a horizontal workflow.
Deleting tracks In both horizontal and vertical workflows, you can use Mission Control to quickly delete child tracks from all folders of the project.

Re-ordering tracks In both horizontal and vertical workflows, you can re-order the mixer tracks by selecting the track in Mission Control and using the arrow buttons. This also moves all audio and assigned recording inputs. Aux and submix tracks can be moved up and down in the same way.

Audio Calculator To figure out required disk space for a duration of audio or vice versa to figure out maximum duration of audio you can record based on available disk space, use Shift+H to open a calculator. You can set units, channel count, samplerate, bit depth and format (WAV or MP3 at various bitrates). Screen reader users (Clara) The Accessible Audio Calculator offers the same calculation as a keyboard-driven window.

While it is always better to record in ReaClassical for traditional recording sessions, you may prefer using a portable recorder for live performances. Further, you might need to import audio recorded by other engineers who used a different DAW.

Smart Import Smart Import brings in audio files that follow a simple naming scheme, working out the track, take and (optionally) session from the filename. It handles both ordinary mono and stereo files and multi-channel files from portable recorders (see Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder).

File Naming The take number must be at the very end of the filename, just before the extension, preceded by an underscore. The "T" (for take) and any zero-padding are optional. The part of the name before the take number is split at underscores: the last part is the track name and anything before it is the session name. Examples (where x represents a digit): sessionname_trackname_Txxx.wav sessionname_trackname_xxx.wav trackname_Txx.wav trackname_xxx.wav Examples of good filenaming include: morning_cello_012.wav (session "morning", track name will match "cello", take 12) day1_morning_cello_012.wav (session "day1_morning", track name will match "cello", take 12) harpsichord_T4.flac (no session name, track name will match "harpsichord", take 4) Examples of bad filenaming include: 005.wav (no track name) violin56.wav (no underscore before the take number) WAV, FLAC and AIFF files are imported. A file named roomtone.wav is always ignored, as it is reserved for room tone. Important Don't skip this renaming step if you want to import files easily from another DAW! Manual import by dragging in material can be time-consuming and may not allow you to use functions like searching by take number.

Importing Ensure that you have first created a horizontal or vertical workflow ReaClassical project. Copy or move source material into the media subfolder inside your ReaClassical project folder (you can also assign a custom import/recording path via Project Settings P). Subfolders are searched too. Either leave the track names blank (recommended) or ensure that track names in the project match the track text in the filenames. If your filenames also contain a session name prior to the track name, the items will be grouped accordingly. Via the top ReaClassical menu, click on Project Management > Smart Import Audio or use shortcut Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I. Choose your options on the Named Tracks tab and press Import. Open Mission Control to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc. The Named Tracks tab shows the workflow of the project, how many new takes and sessions were found, and where the material will be inserted. Files already used in the project are ignored, so you can "smart" import further material into a non-empty ReaClassical project. Material is inserted at the edit cursor. The import is built first and then, if anything already sits at or after the cursor on the folders being imported into, that material is moved later by exactly the length of the import to make room. Only the folders that actually receive imported items are affected: importing into the first source folder does not disturb the destination folder or untouched source folders. If an existing item straddles the cursor, it and everything after it move, and a one-second gap is left after the new material. If the project's track names are all blank, you are first given the opportunity to set the order in which the captured track names are assigned to the mixer tracks by dragging rows into place. Import only these takes (optional) lets you restrict an import to a session name and/or a list of takes such as 1-3,5,11-15. In a horizontal workflow all takes are laid out left to right in the single folder, one session after another. In a vertical workflow, takes are placed in source folders. Choose the Starting folder (the first source folder to use) and a Distribution Mode: One folder per take: within each session, the first take goes in the starting folder, the second in the next folder down, and so on. New source folders are created if the project doesn't have enough. Each further session begins again at the starting folder, to the right of the previous one. Use current folder count: takes are dealt out in turn across all the source folders that already exist from the starting folder downward (take 1 to the first, take 2 to the second, ..., then back to the first folder, to the right of the first round). No folders are created. Round-robin across custom number of folders: the same dealing out, but across the number of folders you enter, creating folders if needed. A preview shows the result, including a warning when new folders will be created. Screen reader users (Clara) The same shortcut opens a keyboard-driven walkthrough, announced through Clara, with an explicit confirmation step before the import happens. If the media folder also contains multi-channel files, you are first asked to choose between Import Takes and Import Polywav.

h: Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder
x: Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder If you use a portable recorder such as a MixPre, you might have a multi-channel combined file (a "polywav"). Smart Import can split these into a set of mono and stereo tracks. The Polywav tab appears in the Smart Import window whenever the media folder contains unused files with more than two channels. The filenames must follow the take-number rule above, with an optional session name but no track name: [sessionname_]Txxx.wav. Every polywav imported in one go must have the same number of channels. Enter a channel composition pattern made of the digits 1 (mono) and 2 (stereo), read left to right across the channels of the file. For example: 2 makes the first stereo pair, and then every remaining pair of channels is also treated as stereo 21 makes a stereo pair followed by a mono channel; the remaining channels are mono 221 makes two stereo pairs followed by mono channels for everything else Once the digits have been used up, the last digit repeats for as many whole groups as still fit, and anything left over becomes mono tracks. ReaClassical checks that the result fits before touching your project, then distributes the takes with the same options as Named Tracks. The channel groups are placed on the tracks of the folder in order: the first group goes to the first track, the second to the second, and so on, so the project needs at least as many tracks per folder as there are groups. Tracks that already have names keep them, so you can set up your tracks first and the channels simply follow their order. Any blank tracks are named after their channels (for example "Ch 1" or "Ch 2-3 (Stereo)"). The Polywav tab works on its own, so a media folder that contains only multi-channel files is fine.

Importing a DDP or PMI ReaClassical can rebuild a full CD track and album metadata layout from an existing master, for checking or remastering. Use a fresh ReaClassical project whose destination folder is empty. Project Management > Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D): choose the DDP's raw audio stream, a file with a .DAT extension (conventionally IMAGE.DAT) Project Management > Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M): choose a Pyramix .pmi pre-master

Manual Import by Dragging In your source folder, select items that should be aligned vertically (for example, every channel for particular take) and drag into the ReaClassical project being sure to drop onto one of the folders created by ReaClassical with a track count that matches the number of files you selected. Choose the option "Same time position on separate tracks" Continue as above for each take Open Mission Control C to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

In addition to built-in REAPER functions, ReaClassical uses a series of keyboard shortcuts to help you easily navigate your classical project. You can of course still navigate by clicking around with the mouse as you would in any REAPER project; the shortcuts are there to make it faster, and to make it possible without the mouse at all. Important: I always make some dedicated time post-recording to get an overview of the recorded material, tidy up the digital notes I took during the session and perform a backup on an external drive as soon as possible.

Whole Project Use Ctrl+Alt+→ (or Ctrl+Alt+←) to see the whole project horizontally and/or Ctrl+Alt+↓ (or Ctrl+Alt+↑) to see everything vertically. If you want to zoom both horizontally and vertically at the same time, use ` (backtick). REAPER's own Home and End keys take you to the start or end of the project. + and - zoom in and out horizontally.

Tracks and Folders The arrow keys move you around the project without the mouse. Each move selects the track and announces it (name, peak level and any mute or solo state): ↓ and ↑: next and previous track within the current folder. In a project with a single track per folder these move between folders instead Alt+↓ and Alt+↑: next and previous folder D: the first folder in the project Moving to a folder makes it the folder you hear (the others are muted) and selects the item nearest the edit cursor. If a special track such as an aux, submix or reference is selected, ↓ and ↑ step through the visible special tracks instead. To jump straight to a track by name, press Shift+J and type part of its name.
