Finding Takes Use Enter on the main keyboard or numpad to quickly search for a take based on the underlying filename of the media item. This will work for any file-naming system that uses numbers before the file extension such as mainpair-T04.wav, cello-spot-take23.flac or even ortfpair(04).wav such as created by Presonus Studio One. Note that if the imported or recorded files have zero-padding that is not a problem. If you have used an item to create an S-D edit, searching for a take will ignore these items and move directly to the original sources. In F5 preferences, you can set to search by item name instead. In the ReaClassical Notes app N, you can override and reset take numbers. These take priority in the search.

Jump to Time Press J to jump to a specific absolute or relative time using right-aligned logic, similar to video editing applications. Press Ctrl+J to do the same within the selected item or a set of consecutive crossfaded items, where an absolute time counts from the start of that selection. Prefix with + or - to make relative jumps from the current cursor position. Colons are ignored, so 1:23:45:10 and 01234510 are read the same way. Once you get the hang of using this input logic, moving to any position is extremely quick!

Some Right-Aligned Logic Examples Input Meaning (based on project frame rate) 100524 Move to absolute position 10m 5s 24f 1141711 Move to absolute position 1h 14m 17s 11f +8 Jump forward by 8 frames -1015 Jump backward by 10s 15f +23000 Jump forward by 2m 30s (and 0 frames)

Items & Markers You can shuffle back and forth between item edges and fades by using ← and → (or Q and W). While editing a crossfade these move through the crossfade, and with an envelope selected they move between its points. More precise item moves: Alt+← and Alt+→: start and end of the selected item Ctrl+Shift+← and Ctrl+Shift+→: first and last item on the track Shift+Q and Shift+W: start and end of the folder Alt+Q and Alt+W: previous and next group of crossfaded items Move between markers by using the , and . keys (by design given on my keyboard they are the same keys that have < and >).

Markers, Regions and Time Selection M adds a marker at the cursor and Alt+M inserts or edits a marker (to give it a name). Ctrl+M deletes the marker nearest the cursor, Ctrl+Shift+M moves the nearest marker to the cursor, Ctrl+Shift+G deletes all generic markers and L opens REAPER's region and marker manager. S-D markers use their own keys; see Editing ; creates a region from each selected item, named after the active take, : creates a region from the time selection, and Ctrl+Alt+R deletes all regions [ and ] set the start and end of the time selection at the cursor, Ctrl+] and Ctrl+[ move the cursor to the start and end of the time selection, and / sets the time selection to the selected items 0 deselects all items

Parents & Children ReaClassical can hide or show children of track folders. This means that editing multi-track classical music can be as easy as editing a stereo track. Making an edit to the parent track automatically makes the same one to all the children too. To show or hide the children, select the parent track and press E. The other benefit is that a whole set of takes can be displayed vertically in the main editing window without too much effort.
Peaks Display To adjust the visual zoom of wave peaks, use Ctrl+↑ and Ctrl+↓. This is purely visual and allows for easier editing of quieter sections.

ReaClassical S-D Editing Toolbar While I designed ReaClassical to be used efficiently with keyboard shortcuts, there is a custom S-D editing toolbar for those that prefer it. However I do highly recommend learning the key strokes as you will find your editing speeds improve dramatically. The floating toolbar can be opened via F6 but will automatically open once when you start source-destination editing. Right-click to set a different icon layout and/or zoom. Hover over the icons to discover what is available.

ReaClassical Top Menu At the top of the arrange window, you will see a dedicated ReaClassical menu (in between Options and Extensions). While not intended to be used as the primary way of running ReaClassical functions, it is an organized way of discovering the individual available functions and learning the keyboard shortcuts. Screen reader users (Clara) Every navigation move above is announced, so no extra step is needed. Use Shift+J to go straight to a track by name, and ! to hear the last announcement again. The announcement shortcuts for take number, timeline position and items in the folder are listed in Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

h: Summary of Track Types in ReaClassical
x: Summary of Track Types in ReaClassical While some of these will be covered later in the manual, it is useful to give a summary of track types you can currently use in ReaClassical. First, we have the regular folder or folder of tracks shown in the arrange window. These are where you record or import takes. Second, we have the mixer tracks designated via M: prefix. These tracks shown only in the mixer are where you adjust the usual track controls such as names, pan, volume, phase, add FX etc. Their names are synced across the project via when added or renamed via Mission Control. Third, we have aux busses designated via @ prefix. You can route mixer tracks to these to use as a reverb bus etc. Fourth, we have submix busses designated via # prefix. You can route mixer tracks to these as a way to collect together microphones from the same orchestral section etc. Fifth, we have a dedicated room tone track where you can place recorded or generated room tone (more on this in the mastering section). Sixth, we have the RCMASTER bus which leads directly to the master REAPER bus. Here you can gain stage into the master bus, add FX etc. Seventh, we have reference tracks which lie outside of the RCMASTER structure thereby allowing the user to quickly make comparisons with other imported material via the audition shortcuts. Next, there is the possibility of a live bounce track. This also lies outside of the RCMASTER structure and is a way to capture a live stereo mix from the RCMASTER track. Note Live bounce tracks are only available when recording in a horizontal workflow. Next, another track outside of the RCMASTER structure is the listenback track. This is a way to monitor musicians, conductors, producers etc who might be far away and need to communicate with the recording engineer via a microphone channel. There is also a playback track (a maximum of one, shown in the mixer only, created muted) that you can send to a chosen pair of hardware outputs and unmute for monitoring with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P. Finally, the master bus itself where again you can set final levels, add FX etc. As mentioned elsewhere, try not to delete the mixer tracks or RCMASTER. But, even if you do by accident, open Mission Control C to recreate them. Important A reminder to do all track management in Mission Control!

Statistics For a complete set of statistics on the ReaClassical project, either for your own information or to assist with billing a client, go to ReaClassical > Utilities > Show Statistics or use the shortcut F1. For example, you might have a billing system that charges clients based on number of source-destination edits, or mixing/mastering based on the final length of the album. Information includes: Album: final album length and number of CD markers Project: project age, session time, total project length, total length of source material, total number of items, number of track folders, number of tracks per folder, number of special tracks and number of regions Edits: number of destination S-D edits and destination item splits FX and automation: total FX count and number of automation lanes Session time is the elapsed time (in hours and minutes) since the project's session timer was started, and can be reset to zero from the statistics window. The window also shows your ReaClassical and REAPER versions. The statistics can be copied to the clipboard. Screen reader users (Clara) With Clara installed, F1 opens Accessible Show Statistics, which lists the same values for you to step through and lets you reset the session timer.

Typing Notes Add project, track and item notes using ReaClassical's Notes window (N, or ReaClassical > Utilities > Add Project/Track/Item Notes). For the selected item you can also set the item name, item rank and take number (with a button to reset it to the number found in the filename), as well as an item note. The take number you set here takes priority when finding takes. Screen reader users (Clara) N opens an accessible Notes window with the same fields. Use Left/Right (or Q/W) to move between items while it is open and Space to play and stop. Item Rank (Ctrl+R) and Item Name (Shift+N) also have their own quick windows.
Manually Coloring Items Use the Colorize function (K, or Colorize Selected Item(s) in the ReaClassical menu) to set a custom color (or remove it) for the selected items.
Folder Structure ReaClassical defaults to placing recorded media in a media subfolder and exports in an Exports subfolder of the project folder, making project file navigation easier.

Automatic Backups REAPER allows for powerful and complex backup routines. ReaClassical sets REAPER's auto-save to every 15 minutes and keeps a limited number of backups. Review and modify these in REAPER's Preferences under Project > Backups to suit your own way of working, including switching to backups and auto saves for a number of unique days.

Folders and Items Duplicate folder (No items) (Ctrl+D) adds a copy of the selected folder's tracks as a new folder, without its items. From a horizontal workflow it first asks whether to convert to a vertical workflow Delete Source Folder (Shift+D) deletes the selected source folder (vertical workflow only; it asks you to confirm) Delete All Source Items (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Delete) deletes every item in every source folder (vertical workflow only; it asks you to confirm) Select All Items in Folder (Ctrl+Alt+A) selects every item in the folder of the selected track Paste (Ctrl+V) pastes items and announces how many were pasted Remove All Item Fades (Shift+F) removes the fades from items whose edges are not part of a crossfade, leaving crossfades intact

Project Tabs Ctrl+Alt+N opens a new project tab and Ctrl+Tab (or NumPad +) switches to the next one. Switching announces the name of the project you land on. Multiple project tabs are the way to make multi-disc albums and to compile edits from several projects; see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing.

Cleaning If in doubt, keep everything! Otherwise, the File > Clean current project directory is an excellent way to reduce the size of your projects. Note that when assigning a session name via the Record Panel Window, currently the above REAPER menu item doesn't search recursively. In a way, this reduces the chances of accidentally deleting precious takes. You can always manually delete but, from experience, it is much better to simply keep everything.

Archiving There are various ways to archive classical music projects. First, you can access the Project Bay by Ctrl+B shortcut. You can then ensure that all media used in the project is contained within the project folder itself. If not, you can select as many as necessary, right click and move/copy into the project folder. After this, you can simply compress the folder as a zip and store on an external drive. A further step to guaranteeing ability to open in the future is to freeze tracks so that plugin effects are baked in (with ability to unfreeze later if possible). Alternatively you can save a copy of the project via File > Save project as..., converting to a format like FLAC and trimming the media as you wish. Finally, one to look out for in the future is Project Archiver. However, I don't believe it is quite ready for prime-time yet and recommend using one of the other methods for now.

Auditioning Folders Audition your material via mouse hover + A on parent or child tracks. The folder under the mouse becomes the one you hear (the others are muted), any record-armed tracks are disarmed, and playback starts from the mouse position. Use hover + Shift+A to play back at a custom rate set via ReaClassical Preferences F5 (default x0.75). Use mixer mute and solo buttons to further customize what you hear. Hover over a reference track for easy A/Bing between your audio production and one or more reference audio files. Tip To quickly remove all record-arming in the project, use mouse hover + A or close the Record Panel.

h: Choosing the Folder from the Keyboard
x: Choosing the Folder from the Keyboard You do not need the mouse to choose which folder you hear. Moving to a folder with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D (see Navigating a Project) makes it the audible folder, and Space plays and stops. Shift+Space plays and stops while moving the edit cursor with the playhead, and Ctrl+Shift+Space returns to the position where you last stopped.

Auditioning Around S-D Markers Once you have set source and destination markers, you can hear them without moving the cursor. Each shortcut selects the relevant folder, makes it audible and plays a short segment: Shortcut Plays 6 / 8 3 seconds from the destination IN / OUT marker 7 / 9 3 seconds from the source IN / OUT marker Ctrl+6 / Ctrl+8 the 3 seconds up to the destination IN / OUT marker Ctrl+7 / Ctrl+9 the 3 seconds up to the source IN / OUT marker Alt+6 or Alt+8 from the destination IN marker to the destination OUT marker Alt+7 or Alt+9 from the source IN marker to the source OUT marker If a required marker is missing, ReaClassical says so. Starting a new audition stops any audition still playing. To compare takes before choosing source markers, see the Source Audition Manager (Z) in the Editing chapter. Screen reader users (Clara) All of these work with the keyboard alone and announce what they are doing, including a message when a marker is missing or when the OUT marker is not after the IN marker.
Source-destination editing is truly anywhere to anywhere. This means you can place your source and destination marker pairs on any folder.

Editing Step-by-Step Ensure that the folder where you want to place the marker pair is selected. The best way to do this is to click on the item where you want the marker. Note that in F5 preferences you can set placement at mouse hover meaning that the desired folder is chosen based on hover position. Set destination IN and OUT markers via 1 and 2 Set source IN and OUT markers via 3 and 4 Press 5 to make the source-destination edit (2-, 3- or 4-point edit depending on how many markers you set), or F4 to make a time-stretched S-D edit (requires all 4 markers), or if only using destination IN marker and both source markers, F3 for an "assembly" or 3-point "insert" edit To finesse the edit, click on the right item of a crossfade pair and press F Screen reader users (Clara) Every marker and edit action announces what it did. If you place a marker on the wrong side of its partner (a source OUT before the existing source IN, for example), ReaClassical deletes the stale marker and says so, so an edit can never silently take far more material than you intended. Use Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4 to move to each marker and the audition keys described in Auditioning to hear them. For crossfades, see Crossfade Editing for Screen Reader Users.

Coloring and Fixing Takes There is no separate "prepare takes" step before editing any more. ReaClassical's editing functions find the matching items on the other tracks of a folder by midpoint matching rather than relying on explicit group IDs, and empty items are cleared out automatically each time Mission Control opens. Auto-color project (Shift+K) colors items by take number or folder. ReaClassical runs it for you at the points where it is needed; run it yourself after importing material by hand. Set No Auto Item Coloring in the F5 preferences to switch it off. Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits (Shift+X) repairs items that should be grouped but have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder, for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items. Select any one of them, run it and choose which track has the correct edits. Every other track in the folder is rebuilt across that group from the reference track's edits, re-pointed at each track's own audio file for the same take number.

Crossfade Editor Since v7.40, REAPER includes an excellent professional two-lane crossfade editor similar in nature to the specialist classical DAWs such as Sequoia and Pyramix. With the improved crossfade editor, users can see the continued "ghost" waveforms of the items beyond the crossfade they enter and likewise the previous waveforms of the items that exit the crossfade. The ability to visually align transients and then position the crossfade just before it is absolutely critical (and fun when you have the tools to do it!). Select the right-hand item of a fade (or hover over the item if Add S-D Markers at Mouse Hover is set in the F5 preferences) and press F to enter crossfade editor mode. Press F again to leave it. The two-lane editor has its own keyboard shortcuts for auditioning and navigating. To audition material, hover the mouse inside the crossfade window and: Press A to audition the crossfade with mirrored pre/post roll based on mouse cursor location Press S to audition just the left item based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position Press D to audition just the right item based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position Use Shift+A, Shift+S or Shift+D to do the equivalent but with a custom playrate as set in F5 preferences. Other shortcuts include: Press E to audition just the top lane based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position Press C to audition just the bottom lane based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position Press Alt+S to audition just the out-of-bounds material left of the xfade Press Alt+D to audition just the out-of-bounds material right of the xfade You can shuttle between crossfades using the Q and W shortcuts (or ← and →). Please see the REAPER manual for more details of what is possible including phase alignment and various view options.

h: Crossfade Editing for Screen Reader Users
x: Crossfade Editing for Screen Reader Users Screen reader users (Clara) REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor depends on seeing and dragging the waveforms, so it is not usable with a screen reader. With Clara installed, F starts a keyboard-driven crossfade mode instead, which gives you the same control over the crossfade: nothing is lost. See Crossfade Mode for all of its keys.

Source Audition Manager When making a source-destination edit, you may not have a list or annotated score from the musicians or producer showing preferred edits. If the decision is left to the audio engineer, this process is very straightforward. First set the source audition mode to checked in F5 preferences. Then, open the Source Audition Manager via the Source Audition button in Mission Control or the Z shortcut. To set up all the source audition pairs, set multiple sets of source in and out markers. You will note that when you start to add a second pair, the source markers are transformed into a take marker "region". The only limitation is that you can only have a single take marker region set per item. This allows the user to quickly reposition the S-D markers by simply setting new ones. If your recorded items each contain multiple passes of the same musical material, consider splitting them via the S shortcut. Use the controls in the window to audition, rank and add notes. Once you have settled on a best take, press the convert button (or place edit cursor within a take marker region and press Alt+Z). Note, that any existing real source pair is converted to a take marker region. Assuming one or more destination markers are already set, you can press 5, F3 or F4 to make the desired edit. Sometimes the suitability of source material is difficult to judge until it is heard with the surrounding destination material. Given that all source markers are stored as take marker regions if inactive, it allows the user to quickly undo an edit and switch to an alternative pair. During auditioning, you can delete individual pairs via the X on the specific table row, as well as delete all source audition markers by clicking Delete All Audition Markers or pressing Alt+Delete.
Other Editing Tips

Making a Crossfade by Hand If two items on a parent track overlap, place the edit cursor somewhere within the overlap and press X to crossfade them. The crossfade uses the S-D Crossfade Length from the F5 preferences (35 ms by default) and is applied to every track in the folder. You can then refine it in the crossfade editor with F.

Healing Edits Select a "patch" edit (one involving all 4 markers over the top of a best take, for example) and press Ctrl+H to heal the edit (restoring the underlying material without splits). Tip This works at any point in the editing process and isn't restricted to the last edit made.

Finding Source Material The items representing a S-D edit are colored according to the source material. However, you can also easily locate source material by clicking on an edited item and pressing Ctrl+F. A color-coordinated source IN and OUT marker pair are placed at the source location and in vertical workflow mode, the associated folder is selected. This function also works across multiple project tabs.

Set Item Playrate with Ripple This function, run via Shift+R, allows you to change the playback rate of a selected item, automatically rippling all subsequent items within the same folder to maintain the integrity of your edits. Select a single item on the folder track, enter a percentage value in the input box, and press Apply & Ripple. In relative mode (the default), the value is applied as a percentage change relative to the item's current rate — so entering 5 makes the item 5% faster than it currently is, while -5 makes it 5% slower. In absolute mode (enable the "Absolute rate" checkbox), the value is always relative to normal speed — so 5 always results in a rate of 1.05x regardless of the item's current rate, and 0 always restores normal speed. The Reset to Normal Speed button is a convenient shortcut to return the item to 1.0x playback rate. Pitch is always preserved during time-stretching. Note that only one item may be selected at a time, as each item requires its own independent ripple calculation. The window also includes a Pitch Adjustment section for correcting intonation without affecting item length or requiring any ripple. Enter a value in semitones and press Apply Pitch — positive values raise the pitch, negative values lower it, and fractional values are supported for fine adjustments (e.g. 0.5 for a quarter-tone). The Reset Pitch button returns the pitch to 0.0 (no adjustment). Screen reader users (Clara) With Clara installed, Shift+R opens the accessible Playback Rate window, a keyboard walkthrough that makes the same rate and pitch changes with the same rippling. Press H in it for examples that fit the current relative or absolute mode.

Automatic Crossfade Protection When performing S-D edits, deletions or ripple deletes, ReaClassical automatically detects any existing crossfades that straddle your marker boundaries and consumes them as part of the resulting edit. This prevents stray partial fades being left behind in your project. This is also useful when quickly iterating through alternative source material: since destination markers persist after an edit and are placed at the exact edit bounds, you can create new source markers and immediately re-edit without worrying about crossfade debris accumulating at the destination boundaries.

Marking Edits on your Scores This is best done using a physical, photocopied score by the conductor or lead musician. I advocate for a “T” system where a large T is inserted into the score at the intended edit point. Either side of the T stem, and under the crossbar, the outgoing and incoming take numbers are written. A wavy crossbar indicates some leeway for where the edit point can be placed. Further notes can be attached underneath the T such as directions for tightening the gap etc.

Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing If you'd like to S-D edit between various open project tabs you can set both the source and destination project markers via Ctrl+Alt+1 (or Ctrl+Alt+2) for destination and Ctrl+Alt+3 (or Ctrl+Alt+4) for source (essentially the same numbers associated with regular S-D markers). The markers can exist anywhere on the tab's timeline but perhaps the very beginning or end would be good to keep them out of the way. The S-D editing itself then works just as for a single tab other than any source markers that are set are not deleted to aid quickly undoing in the destination tab and being ready to reapply the edit. The only rule when using S-D project markers is to ensure that source or destination markers should be paired with the corresponding source or destination project marker. This workflow would, for example, allow you to have multiple project tabs (perhaps one for each symphony movement plus a final destination tab), allowing for both internal editing per tab but after setting the S-D project markers compiling the final edit in the destination tab. To delete all the S-D project markers press Shift+Delete. Also, in multi-tab S-D editing, when regular markers are placed, any other existing versions in other tabs are automatically deleted to ensure that only one version of the marker exists at a time across all open project tabs.

Delete / Delete with Ripple While perhaps not used as often as 3- and 4-point edits, I have created two functions for deletion of material. Delete & Ripple Backspace will delete the material between source IN and OUT markers and ripple material to the right backwards with a short crossfade. Delete Leaving Silence Ctrl+Backspace will also delete but maintain the silence without rippling backwards.

Copy/Move Destination Material to Source Run either the copy Ctrl+Alt+C or move Ctrl+Alt+M version of the function from the S-D editing toolbar (no need to ensure the first track is selected) and the function will copy or move all items and edits from the destination folder directly below to a newly created source folder. This allows for saving versions of finished edits either via iteration (copying so you can continue to make further edits) or fresh (moving so you can compile an alternate version of a best take from scratch). These different edits can then be easily auditioned via A the shortcut. This is similar to a Pyramix-style iterative editing method while still maintaining the destination folder as the uppermost folder.
Promote Source to Destination Select a source folder and press the "promote" icon in the S-D editing toolbar or Ctrl+Alt+P to promote the source folder to the top "destination" position.

h: Add S-D Markers to Edges of Item(s) or Time Selection
x: Add S-D Markers to Edges of Item(s) or Time Selection Used in combination with Delete / Delete with Ripple (Ctrl+Backspace/Backspace), you can quickly set both source markers to the edges of one or more selected items on a parent track or time selection via F12. This is a time-saver when dealing with potential sliver edits i.e. small unneeded leftover edits as a result of multiple rounds of zoomed-out S-D editing. Note that the built-in checks when manually placing destination markers should go some way to alleviating this issue which can easily go unnoticed in other classical music DAWs. Likewise you can use Ctrl+F12 to set destination markers (selected items must be in the destination folder). Note that if using time selection for placing source markers, as for S-D marker placement via 3 or 4, make sure you first have the desired source folder track selected before pressing the shortcut (a good way to do this is to first click on the item involved). You may prefer to set both source and destination markers this way over the more traditional number key shortcuts acting as a sort of hybrid between S-D and razor editing. Also note that if both selected items and a time selection exist, the time selection takes precedence.

Nudging Markers and Items After auditioning a marker, nudge it with Ctrl+, (left) and Ctrl+. (right). Selected items are nudged with Alt+, and Alt+.. Both move by the project nudge amount, which you set with the Terminal command nudge=10 (milliseconds) or under Other Settings in Accessible Preferences. The same keys with the "x modifier" (Ctrl+Alt+, and Ctrl+Alt+. for markers, Alt+< and Alt+> for items) move by the nudge amount multiplied by the modifier amount (Terminal mod=10). Each nudge is announced with the item name and the distance moved. While a crossfade is being edited in crossfade mode, use the crossfade mode nudge keys instead.

Move / Zoom to S-D markers To move to any existing S-D markers use Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2, Ctrl+3 or Ctrl+4. To zoom to any of the S-D markers for more fine-grained placement, use Alt+1, Alt+2, Alt+3 or Alt+4. If you have multi-tab S-D editing set up, these shortcuts will also automatically move focus to the correct project tab.
Delete S-D markers To delete all regular S-D markers, press Ctrl+Delete.

Floating Destination Folder The floating destination folder feature enhances vertical workflow efficiency by dynamically positioning the destination folder just above the selected source folder. This reduces unnecessary vertical scrolling when setting IN and OUT markers for destination and source folders that are far apart in the project. Additionally, this feature is fully compatible with mouse hover S-D editing and when setting source markers to item edges (F12). To enable the floating destination folder, open ReaClassical Project Preferences (F5) and set the corresponding line to checked. For example, with floating destination enabled, place a source IN marker (via 3) on any source folder. The destination folder will reposition itself just above the selected source folder. Add the remaining S-D markers as required. Perform any S-D edits via 5, F4, or F3. Select another source parent and place another marker (3). The destination folder will continue adjusting dynamically. It is worth noting that if the destination folder moves above a source folder, the source marker track number correctly updates to reflect the new order. To disable floating mode, re-open ReaClassical Project Preferences and set Floating Destination Folder unchecked. This will also automatically move the destination folder back to the top of the project.

Razor Editing Because of the potential for visual overlap of markers, I much prefer the REAPER razor edit functionality for vertical take work. It works a lot like the process shown in this Pyramix video. While Pyramix also has additional source-destination marker workflows, I couldn't help but feel that for professional ensembles that manage a high degree of tempo regularity between takes, this method can be extremely efficient. This isn't the document to introduce REAPER razor edits as there are plenty of resources online if you do a simple search. Here we are only concerning ourselves with creation of the razor area across all our pairs and spot mics (REAPER's default shortcut is the rather uninspiring Alt+Right drag). Thankfully, it can become the default editing mode by selecting the razor edit mode on the main toolbar and left-click dragging.

Mixing Scenes Add FX, change routing, and optionally adjust volume, panning etc via Mission Control C Open Mixer Snapshot Manager via Shift+M Create automatically-recalled mixer snapshots tied to items. Before rendering, convert to real automation lanes via Convert to Automation Note If setting a snapshot tied to an unnamed item, the first part of the item's ID will be used as the identifier in the table row.
Mixer Snapshot Manager in Detail

General Workflow Click on an item that you want to be the start of a snapshot or mixer "scene" Adjust any mixer parameter including fader, mute/solo, pan, FX parameters etc Click Set Snapshot.... To make changes, select the item or table row, tweak parameters and click the same button now re-labeled Update Snapshot... By default, switching mixer scenes will happen in a gap in the project during playback. Disable auto recall to treat as a simple mixer snapshot tool that affects the whole project. Filter which parameters are recalled by unchecking boxes at the bottom of the window: volume, pan, mute, solo, phase, width, FX, send levels and send routing. By default a snapshot takes effect in the middle of the gap between items; uncheck Switch mid-gap during playback to switch only at the start of the next item that has a snapshot. Snapshots can only be set on items on the first (destination) folder track, which is the track that recall and gap detection are based on. Important Auto recall runs while the Mixer Snapshot Manager is open. To keep it running after you close the window, check Background auto-recall, which hands recall over to a background process. Once converted to real automation points, auto recall is disabled by design and the window can be closed. Screen reader users (Clara) Select an item on the first folder and press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S (Snapshot Add) to capture a snapshot, or press Shift+M, which opens the accessible Snapshot Settings in place of the Mixer Snapshot Manager.
Copying and Clearing Banks The Mixer Snapshot Manager allows 4 independent banks of snapshots with ability to copy between banks and clear.

Rendering The snapshot manager window relies on real time playback for auto recall. For faster-than-realtime rendering, this will lead to unpredictable results. Therefore, at render time, it is advisable to convert to real automation data. To do so, press Convert to Automation and optionally set which folder to use for gap detection (the conversion will also respect the switching mid-gap checkbox). Mixer, aux and submix tracks with snapshot data will appear in the arrange window along with any active automation envelopes. If items connected to mixer snapshots are moved on the timeline as part of editing, click on the convert button again to get instantly updated automation data. To clear the snapshot automation and return to auto recall via the window while editing and mixing, press Clear All Automation. Automation items that you created by hand on mixer, aux and submix tracks are protected: converting and clearing only replace the automation that the snapshots created.

Volume Automation Ensure that a "Destination" or "Source" track is selected. Make a time selection over the passage you want to change and press I. A time selection is required: changes that run from the cursor to the end of the piece are made with the Mixer Snapshot Manager instead. Set the volume level and optional ramp in/out lengths and click Apply Automation. The ramps lie outside the time selection: ramp in is the time before the selection and ramp out the time after it. While you dial in the level you hear it immediately on playback; ramps cannot be previewed in this way. Check Keep window open after applying to make several adjustments in a row. The first time you create an automation item, ReaClassical engages automation mode: items on the source folders are locked and ripple editing is set to all tracks, so a ripple edit on the destination folder carries the automation along with it. You can switch automation mode on and off yourself with Shift+I or from the ReaClassical menu.

More Advanced Automation Turn on advanced mode to gain access to all envelopes associated with the track including FX parameters. If you also need to automate various aspects of the mixer tracks or special tracks, first make them visible in the track control panel by checking the box on the desired track row in Mission Control. Use I as before.

Editing Automation Items Select an automation item and press Ctrl+I (or right-click on it) to edit its middle value and optional ramp in and out values. You can adjust the positioning by left-click dragging on the item itself. Adjust the middle value length by alt/opt-click dragging on automation item edges. Alt+D and Alt+E show and hide automation lanes, Shift+← and Shift+→ move between automation items and Ctrl+Shift+↑ and Ctrl+Shift+↓ move between envelope lanes. Screen reader users (Clara) Insert Automation (I) and Edit Automation (Ctrl+I) open keyboard-driven windows, the Automation Navigator and Accessible Edit Automation, in which you move between tracks, envelopes and values, and hear the level you are choosing while you dial it in.

General Mixing Workflow Suggestions Set piece-by-piece "scenes" using the Mixer Snapshots Manager adjusting mixer tracks, aux and submix controls and any FX parameters. Make temporary adjustments (for example, volume of spot microphones etc) via the automation function I on tracks with items. For spot microphones that should be mostly muted: 1. Use a time selection + I to reduce to lowest value (-150dB/-inf) for the whole piece or use edit cursor + I at the beginning of the timeline to affect the whole project. 2. Use further time selections + I to set required values and any ramping in and out. Tip Remember that the mixer tracks (the ones starting "M:") are fed by the destination and source folders you see in the arrange window. In other words, any automation you add to destination or source tracks will be filtered through the mixer track state. As an example, if your violin spot microphone channel is set at -5dB via automation but the violin spot mixer track fader is at -40dB, the actual output will be -45dB.

h: Mixing for Dolby Atmos Using Fiedler Plugins
x: Mixing for Dolby Atmos Using Fiedler Plugins If you have the Fiedler Beam plugin on your system, use the Mission Control Enable Atmos that appears to add RCFader plugins and Fiedler Beam plugins to every Mixer track as necessary. This will also pass the current mixer fader values to the RCFader plugin. Subsequent presses of the button will check presence of RCFader and Fiedler plugins, and relative position between them, and synchronize fader values. Use Disable Atmos to deactivate both RCFader and Fiedler Beam plugins on every mixer track.

Mixing with Outboard Gear Use the Mission Control HW Outputs to set direct connections to hardware either automatically or manually. If you do not need connections to RCMASTER, disable using the dedicated button in the main Mission Control window. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T toggles the mute on RCMASTER's own hardware output sends (it mutes all of them if any is unmuted, and unmutes only when all are muted), and Alt+K is Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs.

Mastering in ReaClassical is game-changing. Many features described here are not available in any other classical DAW. I hope that the ReaClassical way saves you much time and helps you look forward to the mastering phase of the project. While automatic DDP generation, automatic room tone function, and professional album reports are the main features here, you will probably find the revolutionary mixer snapshot manager is an extremely efficient way to add auto-recall mixer scenes across your production as well enjoying the ability to quickly reorder album tracks via a simple keyboard shortcuts. Tip If working in horizontal workflow, ensure that there is over a minute's worth of empty timeline between the end of the proposed album and any other source material. Instead, you can also choose to convert to a vertical workflow via Mission Control C.

Basic Mastering Workflow The album is built on the first (destination) folder, so make sure your finished edit is there Remove all names from items on the parent track aside from those you want to be track starts. You can clear all items on the folder track via Ctrl+T Enter track start names via the Notes window N Press Y to open the metadata editor Once happy, use the Render buttons along the bottom of the metadata editor (see Rendering). Note In order to make the process as streamlined as possible for the user before the metadata editor window opens, on first run generic albumwide metadata (the name starts with "@") is added to an unnamed item on the parent folder. If that is not possible, a transparent split is made on the final item of the album.

Metadata Editor in Detail The metadata window allows you to enter all track and album metadata in a single place. Album metadata: title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, genre, identification, language, catalog (EAN/UPC) and message Track metadata: title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, message and ISRC for each CD track ISRC values are filled in automatically from the first track's entry, and the album-wide performer, songwriter, composer and arranger values are filled in from one or more entries in the track table. Check Manual ISRC entry or Manual Contributors Entry to override either. Right-click a field to copy its value to all tracks, to all later tracks, or from the album. Invalid ISRC and catalog entries are refused. Screen reader users (Clara) Y opens the accessible DDP Metadata Editor. ↑ and ↓ move between the tracks, Render Settings, Render, Album and CD Settings, and ← and → choose which metadata type (title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, message, ISRC) is read out for the current row. Enter edits the current cell and stops, so pressing ↓ and Enter repeatedly fills in one field down every track. Ctrl+A applies the current value to every track, Ctrl+R to this and the later tracks, Ctrl+P copies the previous track's value and Ctrl+U copies the album's. Read-only cells, such as the automatic album contributors or the automatic ISRC on tracks after the first, announce why they cannot be edited. CD Settings covers digital release, manual ISRC, pre/post roll and marker offsets. Tip Check the "!" box for CD tracks that you would like to have a visual countdown (length set in F5 prefs). This feature is not available in all CD players.
Recalculate After moving CD start (named) items on the timeline, press Recalculate to refresh marker positions.

Digital Release Only For those wanting to export individual media files only, check the "Digital Release Only" checkbox to ignore the CD offset value set in F5 preferences as well as disable the automatic snapping of markers and regions to CD frames. Then render with the WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 buttons at the bottom of the editor. Note When this mode is enabled, you can still set manual marker offsets using the buttons in the metadata editor.

Repositioning and Re-arranging Album Tracks There are two functions which help with reordering or repositioning tracks. First, and perhaps most useful for producing a classical album, is if you decide that you need to reorder one or more tracks. Select the named item you want to move either in the arrange window or metadata editor (by clicking on the track number) and press Move Album Track Up or Move Album Track Down (Ctrl+← and Ctrl+→ in the arrange window) to switch with the track immediately above or below it in the list. Note that gaps are preserved too. The other situation is when you want to start with uniform gaps between a series of short separate pieces. Use Reposition Album Tracks (Ctrl+Y) and enter a value in seconds. Your pieces are then automatically spaced and items crossfaded are left intact.

Marker Offsets There may be instances when an audience member coughs right before a downbeat or a violinist hits strings before the first note of an otherwise excellent performance. The Add Marker Offset function allows you to adjust the start accordingly (assuming you have some nice recorded or generated roomtone on the dedicated roomtone track). To use, manually drag one or more CD markers to where you want them and then click Add Marker Offsets. It adds the correct offset(s) to the item name(s) automatically and refreshes the album metadata editor. Now, adjustments to an item position followed by a press of Y, maintains the relative CD marker offset to the item start. To remove all marker offsets, click Remove All Marker Offsets.

Multi-Disc Albums Each disc is mastered as its own project, because the album is always built on a project's first folder. Make a project (or a project tab) per disc and run through the workflow above in each one. To compile material from several projects, see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing.
Other Mastering Tips

CUE File and Reports The Exports folder in your project folder collects the album listings: album_report.html and album_report.txt, and a complete technical metadata.txt file (useful for sending to a duplication/replication factory). A CUE file and a CD-Text (.cdt) file are written to Exports/Audio+CUE, next to the audio file made by the Cue Audio render button, so the CUE file's reference to the audio always resolves.

BIN+CUE set Create a BIN/CUE pair (either select regions define tracks and render the whole project or select use only # markers and render by time selection if you don't want the first pre-gap as actual silence at the start of track 1).

Peak and Overs Check Press Shift+P to scan every unmuted track that contains items. The window reports the highest peak level and its position, with a Go to Peak button, and lists every point at or above an over threshold (dB) that you set, each with a Go to button. The scan accounts for item and take volume (including a drawn volume envelope, if SWS is installed) and the faders along the routing chain up to RCMASTER, so it reflects the level arriving at the mix bus. Press Re-scan after making changes. Screen reader users (Clara) Shift+P opens an accessible Peak and Overs Check. On opening and on every rescan it announces the peak position and the number of overs and moves the edit cursor to the peak. You can then browse the overs one at a time, hear each over's level, position and track, and audition the peak.

CD Player Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y to play the album back like a physical CD player. The disc is always the first (destination) folder, and only it is heard. The player is a small window that needs keyboard focus, with buttons that mirror its keys for mouse users. When you switch it off with Escape, the cursor returns to where it was before you opened the player. Key Action P Play, pause or resume S Stop, returning to the start of the disc → / ← Next track / previous track (restarts the current track if you are more than 3 seconds into it) ↑ / ↓ Fast forward / rewind D Enter a track number (more than one digit allowed) 1 to 9 Jump straight to that track T Cycle the time display: track elapsed, track remaining, album elapsed, album remaining R Cycle repeat mode: off, track, album B Toggle Transition Review W Set the pre-roll and post-roll for Transition Review H List these keys Escape Power off Transition Review plays only the joins: the start of the album, every transition between tracks, and the end of the album, each with a pre-roll before and post-roll after (10 seconds and 3 seconds by default). It is the quickest way to hear every splice and gap in a finished album without playing it through. The pregap before track 1 is not included. It reports "Nothing left to review" when it has played the last boundary. Screen reader users (Clara) The CD Player works fully from the keyboard and is announced: it says "Reading disc...", the track and time as you move, "Paused" and "Resumed", "No track N" if you ask for a track that does not exist, "Last track" at the end, the review pre- and post-roll values, and "CD Player off" when you close it.

Loudness In terms of loudness, I personally aim for about -18 LUFS Integrated for my classical albums though it can be as high as -16 LUFS and as low as -20 LUFS. The new loudness JSFX meter in REAPER and my own ReaVision Metering Suite along with the normalization of loudness and true-peak limiting in the render dialog are priceless. It's another reason I couldn't go back to the other classical DAWs at this point.
Further information on DDP For more information about DDP metadata see here (also available via the Render dialog via Format > DDP and clicking on Help).

h: Rendering from the DDP Metadata Editor
x: Rendering from the DDP Metadata Editor Rendering is done with the Render buttons along the bottom of the DDP Metadata Editor window, which you open with Y (Create CD Markers). Each button applies its own settings and renders straight away, without showing REAPER's render dialog. The first (destination) folder is the one rendered, and the files go into an Exports subfolder of the project folder. Button What it renders Where it goes DDP A DDP image (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, triangular dither, as the Red Book standard requires) Exports/DDP/IMAGE.DAT with its companion files Cue Audio The whole album as one audio file to pair with a CUE file Exports/Audio+CUE/ WAV One WAV file per CD track Exports/<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/ FLAC One FLAC file per CD track Exports/<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/ Opus 160 One 160 kbps Opus file per CD track (48 kHz) Exports/<format>_160/ MP3 320 One 320 kbps MP3 file per CD track Exports/<format>_320/ M: Stems One WAV per M: mixer track for each CD track, rendered through the master Exports/Stems_<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/ Custom Opens REAPER's render dialog, pre-filled with your choices to the left wherever you set Files for individual CD tracks are named by CD track number and track name. In these per-track files, album and track metadata (titles, performers, ISRC and so on) is embedded where the format supports it, and if the project's media folder contains cover.jpg or cover.png (or folder.jpg or folder.png) it is embedded as cover art in MP3, FLAC and Opus files. Three dropdowns next to the buttons set the sample rate, bit depth and dither for Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, M: Stems and Custom. DDP always uses the Red Book settings. Opus renders at 48 kHz, and MP3 uses 32, 44.1 or 48 kHz, whichever the chosen sample rate divides into cleanly. The Tracks box limits WAV, FLAC, Opus, MP3 and M: Stems to particular CD tracks, for example 1-3,5; leave it blank to render every track. DDP, Cue Audio and Custom always render the full album. Before rendering, ReaClassical checks your metadata and warns about text that DDP and CD-Text cannot hold (characters outside Latin-1, embedded line breaks), duplicated ISRC codes and tracks without a title. Screen reader users (Clara) The accessible DDP Metadata Editor has a Render Settings row (sample rate, bit depth and dither) and a Render row where you choose the format and then, if it applies, a track range such as 1-3,5. Progress and warnings are announced through Clara. To export every recorded take for the musicians or a producer, see Distributing Takes On Location.

REAPER's Render Dialog You can still open REAPER's own render dialog with R. In it, click on the presets button then All Settings. ReaClassical adds presets for DDP, BIN+CUE, Audio for CUE export, Export for External Resampling, and FLAC, WAV, MP3 and Opus at common sample rates and bit depths. After selecting a preset, you should feel free to change any render settings and perhaps save as a new preset for future use.

Samplerate Now that r8brain free has been introduced as the best quality resampler available in REAPER (I highly recommend double-checking that it is selected when resampling at render time) I feel I can do everything, including DDP creation, without leaving my favorite DAW. However, generating a CUE file via the Create CD Markers function is still useful for all sorts of things and I often create FLAC + CUE for album playback in my media player or WAV + CUE to easily burn a CD at home. The Cue Audio button renders the whole album as a single file next to its CUE file for exactly this.

Dither The Render row offers sample rates of 44.1, 48, 88.2, 96, 176.4 and 192 kHz, bit depths of 16, 24 and 32-bit float, and dither of Triangular, HP filtered, Noise shaping or Off. Dither and noise shaping are applied by the render, so choose Off if you prefer to use RCDither or another 3rd-party dither as the last plugin on the master chain. In that case be sure to keep the master fader at unity.

Loudness & Limiting REAPER has a fantastic rendering feature which allows the user to set a desired loudness and peak / true peak setting. For quick exports that need to meet certain targets (i.e. streaming) this makes things extremely efficient and is very transparent when not set to extreme values.

Dry-run Rendering Another REAPER feature that is outstanding is the dry-run render function which allows for very quick offline loudness and peak checks and much faster than using REAPER's included realtime loudness meter. It is therefore extremely easy to set up compressors, limiters etc in the project and make small adjustments based on the dry-run values and maintain complete control over the process.

Other Rendering Tips Not necessarily obvious to new REAPER users are the special =START and =END markers (make your markers in the usual way and label them accordingly) that constrain the length of the project. Rather than rely on extended silence at the end of items or time selections, the =END marker is a great way to ensure you have the exact amount of lead-out you want at the end of the disc. You will hopefully notice I have included various shortcuts for manually creating regions (single or multiple) from items and time selection (great for quickly generating demo snippets). Also worth noting is that you can still do some (or all!) of your source-destination editing with your track markers in place as the S/D markers have IDs far higher than any classical CD would have and are automatically deleted after a successful edit. As long as you have your ripple-per-track mode engaged, all your existing marker placements and carefully crafted edits will remain intact. But, again, don't manually create CD markers at this point as I include a very powerful tool to make light work of that side of mastering.

When working on projects that combine audio and video, the audio engineer must ensure that high-resolution audio edits remain synchronized with the final assembled video. Several approaches exist: No audio edits required – The simplest case. The video editor is free to select camera angles without concerns about audio sync. Post-edited audio with playback – The promotional video is recorded after the audio has been edited, with musicians miming or playing along to playback via loudspeaker. The video editor has complete freedom to cut between angles without sync issues. This method isn't always feasible. Minor edits in live-recorded video – When video and audio are recorded simultaneously and only minor edits are needed, the video editor can use a zoomed-out shot of the concert hall, a musician's face, or another visual to mask a slight time-stretch while preserving timecode accuracy. Multiple synchronized takes – The most complex scenario. Both video and audio are recorded in multiple takes and synchronized via a timeclock. This is the focus of the following discussion. ReaClassical provides tools to generate an edit list for video editors. Rather than a file for direct import, this list serves as a manual reference. For all recordings, but especially those synchronized to a timeclock, REAPER/ReaClassical retains the timeline start position from the recording. This ensures that absolute in/out source positions can be retrieved even after extensive audio edits. To create an edit list: Perform source-destination edits as usual. Set the desired project framerate in the video tab of Project Settings via P. Export the edit list from the ReaClassical menu under Utilities, using the shortcut for the version you need: Build Edit List (using BWF Start Offset) (Alt+Shift+B) for timeclock-synced projects. It asks for an optional offset in frames, applied to every time in the list. Build Edit List (using source file timing) (Ctrl+Shift+B) to reference positions inside the source audio files. In this case, the audio engineer should provide a single channel of audio to help the video editor locate edit points, and the list also includes the source files used. The edit list opens in your web browser as an HTML table with a Done column for tracking progress. When an offset is used, the page states it in red at the top, so the video editor knows the times have been shifted.

h: Do I need my own REAPER license?
x: Do I need my own REAPER license? ReaClassical installs its own portable copy of REAPER, so there is nothing to download from Cockos first. REAPER itself is separately licensed software: after its evaluation period you should buy a REAPER license from Cockos.

h: Can I install ReaClassical into my existing REAPER?
x: Can I install ReaClassical into my existing REAPER? No. The installer creates a separate, self-contained ReaClassical folder with REAPER and everything pre-configured (resource files, theme, keymap and plugins), and installing into an existing setup, including by importing the ReaPack repository on its own, is not supported. See Install.

h: What if I only want the source-destination editing functions?
x: What if I only want the source-destination editing functions? You do not need ReaClassical for that. ReaEdit is a free, separate package that adds source-destination editing to regular REAPER, with its own manual at reaclassical.com/reaedit. If you use ReaClassical you already have all of these functions, and many more, so you do not need ReaEdit and should not install it.

Is ReaClassical free? Yes. ReaClassical and ReaEdit are free and open source, released under the GNU General Public License version 3. There is no license key, no account and no activation. See Licensing.

h: How many computers can I use?
x: How many computers can I use? As many as you like. There are no seats or machine limits.

Does ReaClassical work offline? The installer needs an internet connection. After that ReaClassical works entirely offline: nothing checks a license or contacts a server while you work. You only need the internet again when you ask for a download: Update ReaClassical, Update REAPER, the Terminal clara command, or an update through ReaPack. REAPER's own projects, of course, are ordinary local files.

h: Can I carry ReaClassical on a USB drive between computers?
x: Can I carry ReaClassical on a USB drive between computers? Yes. A ReaClassical folder is portable, so you can copy it to a USB drive and run it on any computer of the same operating system.

h: Can my school, university or studio use it on many computers?
x: Can my school, university or studio use it on many computers? Yes, on as many computers as you like.

What information does ReaClassical send? None about you or your work. It never uploads your audio or projects. The installer, Update ReaClassical, Update REAPER, the Terminal clara command and ReaPack download files when you ask them to, which is the only network activity. See the Privacy Policy.

Which operating systems are supported? Windows (x64, x86 and ARM64), macOS (Apple silicon, 64-bit Intel and 32-bit Intel) and Linux (x86_64, i686, aarch64 and armv7l, including Raspberry Pi). See Compatibility.

h: Can I use my existing REAPER projects?
x: Can I use my existing REAPER projects? Yes. Open the project and use Project Management > Convert REAPER project in the ReaClassical menu. It converts the project in a new tab, flattens folders, deletes empty tracks and moves effects to the mixer tracks, leaving you to recreate any custom routing in Mission Control. See Converting a Standard REAPER Project.

h: Can I open my ReaClassical projects in regular REAPER?
x: Can I open my ReaClassical projects in regular REAPER? Yes. A ReaClassical project is an ordinary REAPER project: a standard .RPP file with your normal audio files, so it opens, plays and renders in any current vanilla REAPER, on any machine, with or without ReaClassical. Your recordings, edits, crossfades, markers and mix are all still there. What regular REAPER does not have is the specialist ReaClassical tooling that makes the work efficient: the recording workflow, source-destination and crossfade editing, Mission Control, mixer snapshots, the mastering tools, the DDP metadata editor and so on. Those exist only in ReaClassical. If the project uses ReaClassical's own plugins (the RCPlugs collection), install them in the other REAPER too, or regular REAPER will show those plugins as missing.

h: Should I choose a horizontal or vertical workflow?
x: Should I choose a horizontal or vertical workflow? Neither is better; each has its advantages. In a horizontal workflow, recorded or imported takes are arranged left to right in a single folder. A vertical workflow helps organize like material in a recording session: takes of the same musical material are recorded vertically aligned, one folder per take. Functions such as finding a take by number work the same way in both, so choose whichever matches how you like to see your session. You can convert between them later in Mission Control. See Project Setup.

h: Why can't I rename, add or delete tracks the normal REAPER way?
x: Why can't I rename, add or delete tracks the normal REAPER way? ReaClassical keeps a set of linked tracks in step with each other (the folders, the M: mixer tracks, aux and submix busses and the routing between them). Doing track management outside Mission Control breaks that link. If you do it by accident, open Mission Control (C) and it will recreate what is missing.

h: How do I start a recording?
x: How do I start a recording? Select the parent track of a folder and press F9. This opens the Record Panel and arms the folder. See Recording.
Where do my recordings go? Into a media subfolder of the project folder by default. You can change the primary and secondary recording paths in REAPER's Project Settings (P), on the Media tab.

h: How do I give the musicians the takes while I'm still on location?
x: How do I give the musicians the takes while I'm still on location? Press Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes, called Quick Export Recorded Takes in the ReaClassical menu). It exports every recorded take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 into the project's Exports/Distribute_Takes folder, using your mixer settings. See Distributing Takes On Location.

h: How do I import audio recorded in another DAW?
x: How do I import audio recorded in another DAW? Name the files with a track name and a take number at the end, such as cello_012.wav, put them in the project's media folder and run Smart Import (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I). Multi-channel files from a portable recorder are handled on the Polywav tab. See Importing.

h: How do I make a source-destination edit?
x: How do I make a source-destination edit? Set destination IN and OUT markers with 1 and 2, source IN and OUT markers with 3 and 4, and press 5. Press F on the right-hand item of the crossfade to fine-tune it. See Editing.

h: How do I undo or repair an edit?
x: How do I undo or repair an edit? Ctrl+Z undoes the last action. To restore the material underneath an earlier patch edit, select it and press Ctrl+H to heal it. If items that should be grouped have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder, for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items, select any one of them and run Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits (Shift+X).

h: Why do my mixer scenes not sound right in a render?
x: Why do my mixer scenes not sound right in a render? Mixer snapshots are recalled in real time during playback, which does not work for a faster-than-realtime render. Before rendering, press Convert to Automation in the Mixer Snapshot Manager. See Mixing.

h: How do I make a DDP image?
x: How do I make a DDP image? Open the DDP Metadata Editor with Y, fill in your album and track metadata and click the DDP button along the bottom. The result is in the Exports/DDP folder of the project. See Mastering and Rendering.

h: How do I render each CD track as a separate file?
x: How do I render each CD track as a separate file? Use the WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 buttons in the DDP Metadata Editor. Choose the sample rate, bit depth and dither first, and limit the tracks with the Tracks box if you only need some of them. See Rendering.

h: What loudness should I aim for?
x: What loudness should I aim for? That depends on where the music is going. The author aims for about -18 LUFS integrated for classical albums, and anywhere between -20 and -16 LUFS is reasonable. REAPER's render dialog can also normalize to a loudness target and apply true-peak limiting, and a dry run gives you quick loudness and peak values without a full render.

h: Can I use my own plugins?
x: Can I use my own plugins? Yes. Any plugin that works in REAPER works in ReaClassical, and Mission Control lets you add FX to the mixer tracks. ReaClassical also comes with a set of mastering-grade JSFX plugins. See Recommended Free Mastering-Grade Plugins.

h: Can blind and low-vision engineers use ReaClassical?
x: Can blind and low-vision engineers use ReaClassical? Yes. With the Clara accessibility bridge installed, ReaClassical announces what it is doing and provides keyboard-driven windows and modes for every stage of a production. See the Accessibility section.

h: How do I update ReaClassical, and how do I reset it?
x: How do I update ReaClassical, and how do I reset it? Press Shift+U (Update ReaClassical) to receive the latest version of your major release. A new major version needs a fresh install. To return to the settings from first install, use ReaClassical Factory Reset (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F). See Update.

h: Is there a PDF manual, and where do I get help?
x: Is there a PDF manual, and where do I get help? There is no PDF. The manual is online at https://reaclassical.com/manual and a single-page copy is installed with ReaClassical (press H). For support, see Community and Support.

Support Support for ReaClassical is provided on the ReaClassical subforum of the REAPER forum. Please include your operating system, your support info (press Shift+F1 to copy it, then paste) and, if possible, a description of the steps that led to the problem. The Shortcuts Guide A complete, searchable list of every ReaClassical shortcut is available as a web page, generated from the keymap that ships with ReaClassical so it is always accurate. Open it offline from the ReaClassical menu with Shortcuts Guide, or online at https://reaclassical.com/rcshortcuts.html. Type in the search box to filter by action name, mode or key. The Mode column matters. "Normal" shortcuts work everywhere. The other values are keyboard modes with their own keys: Crossfade Mode, Item Edit Mode, Mixer Mode and Recording mode (see Keyboard Modes), and the two-lane crossfade editor's own shortcuts. The same key can mean something different in each mode. Screen reader users (Clara) Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) walks through the ReaClassical menu with a screen reader, announcing the shortcut for each item, so you can explore the available functions without leaving REAPER.

First stop: Reaplugs , with particular mention of ReaLimit which I consider one of the best free transparent limiter available. You could easily mix and master a whole album using only these fine plugins. Others include:

Analysis ReaVision (ReaClassical metering suite). Your one-stop shop for loudness and true peak values as well as adjustable K-meter, goniometer (with adjustable visual boost), phase correlation meter, bitmeter, spectrum analyzer and spectrograph.

EQ RCChannelEQ (ReaClassical Channel EQ, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in ReaPack via my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows Baxandall and Stillwell's RBJ Highpass/Lowpass Filters for broad-strokes EQing. RCMasteringEQ (ReaClassical Mastering EQ, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in ReaPack via my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows Hull2 with added Range drop-down (Classical or Full) for transparent, musical, broad-strokes EQing. ReEQ https://forum.cockos.com/showthread.php?t=213501. An amazing Fabfilter Pro-Q clone for detailed EQ work. Also comes with ReSpectrum which is an excellent analyzer. Both are included with the ReaClassical install.

Compression RCCompressor (ReaClassical compressor, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from Express Bus Compressor by Stillwell. Default settings and ranges tuned to classical music with auto release. Use as an insert. RCParallelK (ReaClassical parallel Katz compressor, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Also uses DSP from Express Bus Compressor by Stillwell to recreate the Bob Katz transparent parallel compression settings. There's only a make-up gain slider as everything else is baked in (-50dB threshold, 2.5:1 ratio, 1ms attack, peak detection mode). Use on a dedicated compressor bus and adjust the gain slider to taste (with the compressor signal somewhere between -15dB and -5dB lower than dry signal according to Katz).

Limiter RCLimiter (ReaClassical limiter, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from Smooth Limiter by Geraint Luff to which I added 4x oversampling code. Defaults are tuned to classical music with true-peak and look-ahead functionality. Adjust the release to taste.

Reverb Algorithmic: For a free option try my RCReverb (ReaClassical reverb, port of zita-rev1, included in the ReaClassical portable install as part of RCPlugs collection). For paid options, ValhallaDSP Room and Vintage Verb, Fabfilter Pro-R, Voxengo Sobor, Acon Digital Verberate 2 and Sonible smart:reverb are all excellent non-iLok options for classical music and work seamlessly via yabridge on Linux. Convolution: Convology XT (also runs perfectly at time of writing via yabridge on Linux) coupled with the Samplicity Bricasti M7 impulses. There are other free convolution plugins to use but, whatever the plugin choice, the Bricasti impulses in true stereo are fantastic and sound almost identical to the presets of the well-regarded Liquidsonics Seventh Heaven Professional.

In File > Project Templates you will find a room tone generation template. The method is derived from here. To create endless room tone based on the venue you recorded: Click Browse in ReaVerb and select your few seconds of recorded reverb. Enable the FX on the first mixer track Adjust the length of the included region to the length of your live album Render using Bounds > All project regions Save the rendered file as roomtone.wav in your ReaClassical project's media folder. When you add a Room Tone track via Mission Control, ReaClassical imports roomtone.wav onto it automatically (it is never overwritten if the track already has an item). Each time you run Create CD Markers via Y, the room tone item is trimmed to end at the =END marker, or at the end of the last item on the first folder if that marker does not exist yet, and automation-based fades are added to coincide with opposite fade types on the first track, creating perfect crossfades into room tone and back without any fuss. If the room tone audio is shorter than the album, you are warned how many seconds short it is.

Windows For a modern Windows 10/11 setup, required tweaks are minimal. Ensure that you are using 'High Performance' or ideally 'Ultimate Performance'. which, if not available, can be activated by opening a command prompt and pasting: powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61 You can then select it from the usual power plan dialog. For best device performance, remember to use the ASIO drivers that were included with your audio interface. Consider disabling your network card during mission-critical recording. For further tips see Microsoft's Unofficial Windows 10 and 11 Audio Workstation build and tweak guide. Of particular interest is Part 3 which discusses what not to do (including not setting your processor scheduling to 'background services').

MacOS Performance should be excellent out of the box. Remember to disable energy saving (System Settings > Energy on recent macOS, or System Preferences > Energy Saver on older versions) so that sessions are not interrupted. Consider disabling your network card during mission-critical recording. If you are experiencing any audio issues while in your DAW, for tips see Focusrite's optimization page.

GNU/Linux Linux users should visit my Arch Pro Audio Guide. Performance out of the box on Linux is getting better with every kernel release and is on par or better than Windows. As a starting point, ensure that your username is set up for realtime privileges (step 3), that the threadirqs kernel parameter is set (step 4) and that you are running the performance CPU governor (step 5). Check that your kernel is fully preemptible too (see the guide's introduction). To make things even easier, consider using a dedicated audio/video distro like AVLinux or Ubuntu Studio where everything is already set up for you.

Cross-platform The good news is that REAPER and ReaClassical run on many different architectures and operating systems. You should always be able to open up a project on another machine even if it is running a different OS. Plus, ReaClassical includes various mastering-grade plugins in JSFX format that run on all architectures.
